utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: This is the appeals hearing in the case of the Prosecutor against Mladen Naletilic, also known as Tuta, and Vinko Martinovic, also known as Stela. I will briefly now summarise the appeals which are pending before the Appeals Chamber and the manner in which we will proceed today. The appeals deal with crimes related to the HVO attacks on Sovici, Doljani, Mostar and Rastani in south-western Bosnia-Herzegovina during the period from April 1993 until January 1994. Naletilic, Martinovic and the Prosecution appeal from a judgement rendered on 31st March, 2003 by Trial Chamber I composed of Judge Liu and Judges Clark and Diarra. The Trial Chamber found Naletilic guilty on charges of persecution on political, racial and religious grounds as a crime against humanity, Count 1; of unlawful labour as a violation of the laws and customs of war, Count 5; as torture as a crime against humanity, Count 9; torture as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Count 10; wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Count 12; unlawful transfer of a civilian as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Count 18; wanton destruction, not justified by military necessity as a violation of the laws or customs of war, Count 20; and plunder of public or private property as a violation of the laws or customs of war, Count 21. Naletilic was sentenced to a single sentence of 20 years of imprisonment. The Trial Chamber found Martinovic guilty on charges of persecution on political, racial and religious grounds as a crime against humanity, Count 1; inhumane acts as a crime against humanity, Count 2; inhumane treatment as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Count 3; unlawful labour as a violations of the laws or customs of war, Count 5; wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Count 12; murder as a crime against humanity, Count 13; wilfull killing as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Count 14; unlawful transfer of a civilian as a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions of 1949, Count 18; and finally plunder of public or private property as a violation of the laws or customs of war, Count 21. Martinovic was sentenced to a single sentence of 18 years of imprisonment. Naletilic and Martinovic filed notices of appeal on 29 April 2003. The Prosecution did so on 2nd May 2003. I will now briefly summarise the grounds of appeal. Naletilic brings 40 grounds of appeal. Grounds 1 through 39 allege errors in the Trial Chamber's factual findings in relation to each of Naletilic's convictions, including those findings that deal with his position as a commander. Naletilic also alleges that the indictment was vague for certain incidents. He further alleges errors in the admission and evaluation of evidence and in the Trial Chamber's ruling on certain motions. Ground 40 concerns his appeal from sentence. In particular, under his 17th ground, Naletilic alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that certain acts constituted torture because, according to him, the evidence was insufficient to establish that they rose to the requisite level of seriousness. On 2nd September 2005, Naletilic sought leave to submit a pre-submission brief on torture. The Appeals Chamber denied leave on 13 October 2005 on the basis that the pre-submission brief raised a whole new ground of appeal which was outside Naletilic's notice of appeal and that good cause did not exist for amending the notice of appeal. Martinovic brings three grounds of appeal. Under his first ground Martinovic alleges errors of law relating to the Trial Chamber's finding of an international armed conflict and to the permissibility of alternative charging and of cumulative convictions. Under his second ground, Martinovic alleges that the indictment was vague with respect to certain incidents and alleges errors in the Trial Chamber's factual findings in relation to each of his convictions. His third ground concerns his appeal from sentence. The Prosecution originally brought four grounds of appeal. By notice of 30 September 2005, the Prosecution withdrew its second ground of appeal regarding unlawful labour. Under its first ground, the Prosecution alleges errors in the Trial Chamber's finding that there was insufficient evidence that certain acts were committed on racial, political, religious grounds for the purposes of persecution. Under its third ground of appeal, the Prosecution alleges that the Trial Chamber erred in holding that deportation requires the transfer of persons across a state border. Under its fourth ground of appeal, the Prosecution alleges errors by the Trial Chamber in applying cumulative convictions to persecution and another Article 5 crime. On 6 October 2005, the Prosecution filed a confidential motion for the admission of additional evidence on appeal pursuant to Rule 115. The Appeals Chamber granted it on the basis that the proffered evidence was unavailable at trial and that had it been available, it could have shown that Naletilic's conviction pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute for the torture of Witness Z was unsafe. It would be most helpful if the parties could address this additional evidence in their submissions, bearing in mind the protective measures that are in place. During the hearing, the Appellants' counsel may argue the grounds of appeal in the order they consider most suitable for their presentation. I wish to note, however, that by the Scheduling Order of 16 September 2005, the Appeals Chamber has invited the parties to further develop their submissions on the following alleged errors which the Scheduling Order sets out in greater detail: (1) is the vagueness of the indictment for several incidents; (2) is the definition of deportation; (3), admission of evidence secured by a search warrant; (4), admission of evidence in support of the Prosecution's rebuttal case; (5), Naletilic's mens rea as a superior regarding the activities of ATG units in Ljubuski and Mostar; (6), unlawful labour in the area of responsibility of the Vinko Skrobo ATG; (7), the use of human shields on 7 September 1993; and (8), the use of detainees to loot private property. The parties have also been invited to clarify a list of small points which was communicated to them on 16 September 2005 in which -- does not need to be restated here now. These invitations are made - I want to stress - without prejudice to any matter the parties or the Chamber may wish to raise and in no way constitute an expression of an opinion on the merits of the appeal. I would now like to recall the criteria applicable to errors of fact and law alleged on appeal. The appeal is not a trial de novo and the Appellants must not merely repeat their case from the trial level. Rather, in accordance with Article 24 of the Statute of this Tribunal, the Appellants must limit their arguments to alleged errors of law which invalidate the decision or alleged errors of fact occasioning a miscarriage of justice. Additionally, it should be recalled that the Appellants have an obligation to provide precise references to materials supporting their arguments on appeal. This hearing will proceed according to the Scheduling Order issued on 16 September 2005. Counsel for Naletilic will present his submissions this morning until 10.45, for one hour 30 minutes. Following a 30 minutes' pause, counsel for the Prosecution will present his response, again for an hour 30 but there will be a pause in between for lunch. And therefore, and afterwards, counsel for Naletilic will have time to reply, 30 minutes in the afternoon. Then we will proceed with the appeal of Martinovic. And we will conclude the hearing before 6.00 tonight. The hearing will continue tomorrow for the other comments. And we will conclude tomorrow evening. It will be most helpful to the Appeals Chamber if the parties could present their submissions in a precise and clear manner. Of course, I wish to remind the parties that the Judges may interrupt the parties at any time to ask questions or they may prefer to ask questions following each party's submission. Having said this, about the manner in which we will proceed today, I would now like to invite counsel for Naletilic to present submissions in support of his appeal. Mr. Farrell.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: If I can just indicate to the Court that with your leave I'll excuse myself with Mr. Tracol. Thank you.

utterances.text: Sure. So counsel for Naletilic has the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Honourable Chamber, just a preliminary matter is that we spoke with the OLAD last week concerning an interpreter to be here with us in the courtroom so that we could communicate with our client, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta. He spokes no English and we spoke no B/C/S. The interpreter, Marko, was supposed to be here a little before 9.00, and I am unsure where he is, if he's down in the lobby or if they didn't let him come up. I left my -- obviously my cell phone in the Defence counsel room, so if he's trying to call me I wouldn't know it. I just want to bring that to the Chamber's attention because I think it's kind of an important issue to have -- to be able to communicate with our client or our client be able to tell us or ask us or direct us to do certain things. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: May I ask the Registrar to clarify this point?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can go out and search for this gentleman perhaps, if you wish. We don't know whereabouts of this interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Well, I would suggest that the Registrar or the usher go to look for the interpreter. But in the meantime, I think counsel for Naletilic can start presenting the case because the accused can follow in any case the presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Judge, and that was going to be my suggestion. May it please the Court, members of the Prosecution and members of the Defence, again my name is Matthew Hennessy and I have the privilege of representing Mr. Naletilic here on appeal. I'm going to first present an outline of what we intend to cover and just in our presentation here, of course, we stand by our brief and certainly do not withdraw any of the points presented in it. But what we will cover -- what we will cover will ultimately address what convictions should stand and what the ultimate sentence should be, as the Court has already stated and is well aware of, the sentence given was a single sentence of 20 years. At the conclusion of our presentation here later today, we will be asking the Chamber to reform judgement and sentence and sentence to no more than eight years' incarceration. We will begin -- I will begin by discussing command, Mr. Naletilic's command position and the evidence of it, move on to evidence supporting, or not, his mens rea in connection with the Ljubuski and Mostar points. In connection with Ljubuski I'll also, as the Court has invited us to, discuss the impact of the Prosecution's latest filed Rule 115 motion. I'll then move on to the Rados diary points, PP928. We will then discuss mistreatment of prisoners focussed mainly on torture. Discuss the vagueness of the indictment, specifically as to the Mostar unlawful transfer convictions, and as to the Ljubuski prison events. I'll also talk about sentence and how this, as we contend, this 20-year sentence is out of step with the continuum of convictions that have come out of this Tribunal. Mr. Meek will cover the search warrant issue that we've raised and Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. also our objections to the admission of Prosecution Exhibit PP704. He will also discuss the impact of the evidence of Falk Simang and related points, plunder, forced labour, and he'll also summarise in greater detail factual errors that we have presented. There is some overlap between the appeal of Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic, overlap that we see involves international armed conflict and deportation. Both of those points will be covered by Mr. Kerns in due course. Moving now to command position, in paragraph 96 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Naletilic was not the operative commander of the Convicts' Battalion but rather was the overall commander. While we don't disagree with that finding, we don't agree with it entirely. We certainly do not disagree that he was not the operative commander, and I'll note that all liability under 7(3), superior liability, is continued upon operations that were conducted throughout the area relevant to the indictment, and as was already found by the Trial Chamber, he was not an operative commander but rather a, quote/unquote, overall commander. What we disagree with is the evidence supporting this concept that overall commander meant he had effective control or actual control of the actual individuals who participated in the operations. What is true, and is not reasonably in dispute, is that Mr. Naletilic founded the Convicts' Battalion. We take issue with the fact that he was a commander all the way through the period -- the relevant period of the indictment. What is certainly true, and we do not dispute, is that Mr. Naletilic remained a man of influence throughout the time. But being that he was not an operative commander, we contend that the evidence does not support the contention of the Prosecution that he was in a position to know or have reason to know what members of the battalion which he had formally founded were doing during the time relevant to the indictment. That brings me to mens rea, knew or had reason to know, which is our ground of appeal 21. As to -- I'm going to begin with the Ljubuski events, the Ljubuski prison. In paragraph 428 of the trial judgement, the Trial Chamber attributed 7(3) responsibility to Mr. Naletilic because he -- they said, they found that he had reason to know that there was a high risk, high risk, that Convicts' Battalion members would go to the Ljubuski prison seeking revenge for prior events. I suggest, as a preliminary matter, that the Trial Chamber's statement that 7(3) responsibility is attributable based upon this high risk is -- indicates a misapplication of the law of mens rea with respect to 7(3), which is set out fully in the Celebici appeal judgement. It's know or had reason to know. This high risk, this good chance or high risk is, I suggest, at odds with the degree of certainty which an individual alleged commander should have in order for 7(3) responsibility to be triggered. But let's further examine the evidence which we contend does not support a finding of mens rea in connection with Ljubuski, the Ljubuski prison. The -- in addition to this so-called or perceived high risk, the Trial Chamber found that Mr. Naletilic's knowledge, if you can call it that, that things may happen, if bad things may happen, crimes may be committed in the Ljubuski prison began on the road to Ljubuski from Sovici. The testimony was that along the way on that road a bus was stuck in the mud and that bus was carrying prisoners from Sovici to Ljubuski. Soldiers were mistreating one of the prisoners, a Witness Y. Mr. Naletilic arrived during the mistreatment of that prisoner and stopped the mistreatment. My point being is that the two -- the event which the Trial Chamber stated that must have created a high risk or that Mr. Naletilic would have known there was a high risk of mistreatment that in fact what that event -- that event along the road to Ljubuski was actually evidence to the contrary, that he had stopped it and had no reason to think it would continue. So this concept of high risk, while one misplaced, is not supported by the record. We are moving into problems with the -- which Mr. Meek will address regarding PP704, this list of members, supposed members, of the Convicts' Battalion, that list being from November 1993. The reason I come to that is a final element of the Trial Chamber's findings as to Mr. Naletilic's mens rea as to Ljubuski prison involved the fact that the Trial Chamber found that Romeo Blazevic, Ernest Takac, a person named Robo and Ivan Hrkac actually committed the various crimes there at Ljubuski prison. This document, PP704, was used by the Trial Chamber to establish that those names, that those people, were at relevant times members of the KB, Convicts' Battalion. Mr. Meek will speak more specifically about how that particular document should not be used in the manner in which the Trial Chamber used it. Also he will speak about the fairness of using that document, that is based upon how it was found, using the search warrant, and as I said, Mr. Meek will address whether that document should have been admitted at all. But suffice for my purposes here as to mens rea, there was not sufficient evidence, not a sufficient predicate established to show that the people on that list, the 282 people, is what the Trial Chamber found at one point, that those 282 people were all members of the KB at all relevant times. PP704 does not set out when these individuals who were on the list became members and specifically does not identify when Romeo Blazevic, Ernest Takac, the person named Robo or Ivan Hrkac, when they were members of the KB for purposes of attributing any of their conduct to Mr. Naletilic in the sense of that he knew or had reason to know what they might be doing. 704, PP704, also is important now, I told the Court or the Chamber I would be mentioning this, based upon the Prosecution's recent 115 filing. Important in my view to the Trial Chamber's determination of Mr. Naletilic's mens rea as to what was going on at Ljubuski prison, and mind you, between May and September of 1993, not -- not a discrete dates or discrete short periods of time from May to September. What the Trial Chamber found and the Chamber will see this in the paragraph -- it's paragraph 478 -- excuse me, 428 and just before, two or three paragraphs before that, in the trial judgement, is reference to a Ivica Kraljevic, who the Trial Chamber found in my view there is no other way to read the judgement, that the Trial Chamber found was a member of the KB, the Convicts' Battalion, at all relevant times for the indictment. And here is the implication of such a finding. Here is the implication of such a finding. If a member of the KB were in charge of the Ljubuski prison and members -- and there are people inside that Ljubuski prison who are on this 704 list, and by the way, this -- the name Ivica Kraljevic, was on the PP704 list as well, that if the warden of the KB is letting other people who are on this same list into the prison for purpose of committing crimes, then the connection, the mens rea, well, that may actually be a fair leap. But if on the other hand -- if and we now know this to be true, the warden, Ivica Kraljevic, of the Ljubuski prison, was not a KB member, was not a KB member at all. That's what the Prosecution's recent 115 filing establishes. It also establishes, it also establishes, that this warden, Kraljevic, did not come to be warden until July or August 1993. The importance of that being -- the importance of that being almost all, rather, all but one of the -- all but one of the crimes attributed to Mr. Naletilic via 7(3) relating to Ljubuski prison, all but one occurred, if they did, before this Kraljevic became warden. So the Trial Chamber's findings as to Ljubuski prison entirely, entirely, need to be reviewed because what happened was -- and specifically, and it's within our point, that this Kraljevic, the true warden, not being a member of the KB, starting in September or August, he certainly was not under even any possible command of Mr. Naletilic, and Mr. Naletilic therefore should not have known it or nor should he have reason to know how this third party was running his prison. And, before he became warden, we have no evidence as to who the warden was, so between May and August of 1993, there is no evidence as to who was running that prison. However, what the Trial Chamber did was attribute 7(3) liability from May to September, 7(3) liability on Mr. Naletilic from May to September 1993 based in large part on the fact that a member of the KB was running that prison. We now know that not to be the case. So to summarise the Defence's view now of what the best state of the evidence could be relating to Ljubuski prison is that some random acts, random criminal acts, were committed by people inside the Ljubuski prison, but that there is no evidence or even -- at best insufficient evidence, to establish who was in control of either the prison or of the individuals who committed such acts. Either way, the mens rea as to any proof of mens rea as to Mr. Naletilic is woefully lacking. Next, as to Mostar, mens rea as to Mostar. Paragraph 88 of the judgement uses as is common throughout the judgement, uses PP704 again to conclude that every member on that list, every person on that list, was a member of the KB throughout all relevant periods. The -- I point that out now because as to Mostar, there were -- and this really relates to -- and I'll address this further, later in my discussion. But as to the mens rea for Mostar that really relates to two convictions for forcible transfers, the one time period being from June 12 -- excuse me, June 13 to 14, 1993 and September 29, 1993. That what the Trial Chamber did was use PP704 to establish that people on the list, PP704, who may have been forcing the transfer of individuals from Mostar in June and September, the Chamber used PP704 to attribute mens rea to Mr. Naletilic that he knew or had reason to know what they were doing on those two discrete dates. Well, point out again that this list is from November 1993, and there is no indication on PP704 as to when the individuals on the list came to be on the list, so it is -- it is not a leap of logic but a leap of faith which led - I respectfully submit - the Trial Chamber to find that members on the people listed on PP704 were under Mladen Naletilic's control in June and September 1993. I also point out that that leap, that leap of faith that I'm calling it, is at odds with what I say is a correct statement of mens rea in the trial judgement at paragraph 116, that in order to establish mens rea, that an individual for 7(3), an individual must know or have reason to know, as to each -- each particular event, each atomic event, so that using a blanket document such as PP704, which shows a list after the fact does not establish who were members at the time of the events. Moreover, the finding that Mr. Naletilic controlled the individuals in June and September 1993, as to the forcible transfers in Mostar, that finding, I suggest, is at odds with another finding of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 84, wherein the Trial Chamber specifically found that once ATG units were sent to a front line, and Mostar was a front line, once an ATG unit was sent into operations, they were -- the ATGs, and the reason I bring that up, PP704 again, PP704 listed not only purported KB members but also members of ATG units in theory who were subordinated to the KB. This goes to my ground of error 7 -- excuse me, ground of appeal 7, that the -- when the ATG units, once were activated and sent to a particular region, the area commander assumed control of them. They did not then -- they took their orders from the area commander, and that's what paragraph 84 found, yet at the same time the Trial Chamber attributes mens rea and 7(3) responsibility to Mr. Naletilic for operations that were conducted after the ATGs were deployed to area commanders. There is a disconnect in that element of control and in the element of mens rea. I'm going to mention now, just as preface to what I expect Mr. Meek to address more fully and that is the testimony of Falk Simang in connection with establishing or, as we say, did not establish mens rea in connection with the unlawful transfers found in paragraph 571, for June 13 and 14, and September 29, 1993, that -- and the Chamber asked us a question or may be it was the Senior Legal Officer transmitted a question to us regarding what evidence there was as to whether Falk Simang participated in the June 13/14 transfers from the Mostar area, and the question was what the Trial Chamber -- did the Trial Chamber found that he participate -- did the Trial Chamber find that he participated in those transfers or in those operations. I refer the Court, and I've transmitted this already to the Prosecution in response to a question he asked, that what the Court did at paragraph 556 in relation to the June 13 and 14 transfers is that it referred back to an earlier paragraph, paragraph 91 of the judgement, paragraph 91 in the judgement, where the Trial Chamber found that -- or rather expressly relied on Falk Simang and Ralf Mrachacz to establish that -- to find that Mr. Naletilic had control at all times of all ATGs. So in response to the question asked by the Chamber, the trial judgement or the Trial Chamber did not specifically state that Falk Simang was part of the June 13/14 operation there in Mostar but by implication the reasonable inference is, given the fact that they are relying on Falk Simang's testimony to support that Mr. Naletilic was a superior to those who actually did carry out the operation, it's a fair inference that they certainly may have so found, though not expressly concluding. As I said, Mr. Meek will discuss more as to the weight and the credibility of the testimony of Falk Simang.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Just a moment. Judge Schomburg, you want to put a question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. In conclusion of your submissions, is it true that your fall-back position would be that as explained in footnote 233, based on the testimony of your witnesses NQ and ML that KB was a small unit with about 60 soldiers only, and are you at odds with the finding of the Chamber in para 48, that there were four professional units, the KB, the Baja Kraljevic unit, Ludvig Pavlovic unit and Ante Bruno Busic unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Well, fall-back position, I would not characterise what I'm just guessing as a fall-back position. Our position is, is that Mr. Naletilic, though he was certainly the charismatic founder, and the KB, the Convicts' Battalion vicariously enjoyed his charisma throughout the time period relevant to the indictment, that whether the KB had 282 or 60 is of less import to our position than whether Mr. Naletilic knew or had reason to know what the members were doing. That's why I pointed out in the beginning of my discussion of mens rea, that he, as the trier of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fact, the Trial Chamber, found, was not the operative commander but an overall commander. Now, perhaps to be more clear, my dispute is with what overall commander means. Our position is that overall commander does not mean that he had the sort of mens rea, the sort of knowledge, knew or had reason to know, as to whoever may have claimed to be a member of the KB or whoever may have claimed to be a member of any ATG unit in theory subordinated to the KB. So the disconnect is not with the numbers but rather with the degree of control and degree of knowledge. Further, as to mens rea, proof of mens rea in Mostar, and this goes to Falk Simang's testimony, I'm speaking now specifically about Count 20, a conviction for plunder under 7(3), Count 20, as to Mladen Naletilic, occurring May 9, 1993. The Chamber based -- the Trial Chamber based its finding that Mladen Naletilic was responsible for plunder based in large part on Falk Simang's testimony which was that he saw Mladen Naletilic, Ivan Andabak, and Mario Hrkac, otherwise known as Cikota, together there on May 9, May 9, 1993, in Mostar, and they, according to Mr. Simang, witnessed people committing plunder, looting homes. It is uncontroverted in the record that Cikota was dead on April 20, 1993. The testimony of Falk Simang is at odds with objective fact. So attributing 7(3) responsibility for plunder based upon Falk Simang's testimony that Mr. Naletilic was present with a dead man on May 9, 1993, should not support a conviction for plunder, and I say that -- And here is our interpreter. I thank you -- thank you for the Chamber's assistance. Just one brief moment while we sort out -- May I continue? Thank you. To conclude as to mens rea, the evidence -- evidence used by the Trial Chamber, that evidence being the testimony of Falk Simang, does not support mens rea -- does not support a finding that Mladen Naletilic knew or should have known about anyone committing plunder in Mostar on May 9, 1993. Moving now to the Rados diary. The Rados diary, our complaints here are at grounds of appeal 6 and 8. Our complaint really here is twofold. One, the document should never have been admitted, even if it was attempted to be admitted in the Prosecution's case in chief. Second, if admissible at all, it certainly should not have been admitted in their rebuttal case. First, and there is -- and I'll admit to this, this trick of rhetoric, and I don't mean that in an accusatory way in a sense with my learned friends from the Prosecution, but I have characterised the Rados diary as a witness statement. I have characterised it as such. By characterising it as such, I say that Rule 92 bis should govern its admissibility or not. The Prosecution has characterised it merely as a document whose admissibility should be gauged by Rule 89. I suggest that my view of the document is more reasonable, and I say that based upon the pervasiveness of the use of the document, the Rados diary, throughout the trial judgement, and that alone gives you an idea as to how the Trial Chamber considered the document. They considered the document as live cross-examined testimony, in my opinion. And if there were any doubt, I suggest that the Chamber review Judge Clark's statements when the trial judgement was presented. In the transcript, she refers to Mr. Rados, recall, let's recall first what the Rados diary was purported to be. The Rados diary was purported to be a contemporaneous journal, if you will, by a soldier in the area of events relevant to the indictment. Of course, Mr. Rados never testified at trial. But what Judge Clark said in her statements there in presenting the judgement was that Mr. Rados was a brave and humble man. How could you -- how could -- how is it possible to make such a character judgement if what this really is is a document admissible under Rule 89? What we have here, the way that this document was treated, it was treated as live cross-examined testimony and given that weight throughout. So though, yes, I'm pitching a level of generality and I'm making conclusions from that, that level of generality being that this document was a witness statement which did not comply with Rule 92 bis, nor did it comply with the -- with the practice direction about 92 bis, and let's imagine how the Prosecution could have complied with 92 bis. If they had taken the document, which they had, and presented it to Mr. Rados, they could have had him verify, pursuant to the practice direction for 92 bis, that the statements therein were true in front of an authorised person. That was not done. Given the fact that the Trial Chamber treated this, the fact that the Trial Chamber treated this as cross-examined, live testimony, I suggest that means it should be treated or its admissibility should be reviewed under the guidelines of Rule 92 bis, and as I've already said, Rule 92 bis was not complied with. It should not have come in, in any respect, in any part of the Prosecution's case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You made reference to a statement of Judge Clark that this man was a brave and humble man. Unfortunately, I haven't found this in the judgement. Characterisation of the diary is to be found in footnote 54. Is it maybe only the oral statement of Judge Clark?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: So it's not in the written judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: But I'm using her statements to -- and my colleague is confirming it was in -- it was in the summary that she read orally at the time judgement was presented to the Defendants. But I view that as important that that gives us a look into the Chamber's mind and how they were using this document. As I said, it should not have come in at all. But if it were admissible at all, it should not have come in as it did in the Prosecution's rebuttal case. The Celebici Appeals Chamber was very clear on this. Celebici Appeals Chamber says that rebuttal evidence must relate to a significant issue arising directly out of Defence evidence which could not have been anticipated. Could not have been anticipated. I do not now guess what the Prosecution will reply with, but I note for the Chamber that, first, the Prosecution was aware of this document, the Rados diary, PP928, in March of 1998, March 1998. They, the Prosecution, offered a portion of the document at the close of their case in chief. It was not as though they did not anticipate its usefulness if it was useful at all. They were aware of it years before trial began and they offered it in their own case in chief. That it was not entirely admitted in -- if -- and my recollection now is that it was not admitted at all in their case in chief but -- that is, a portion of it, it was not admitted in its entirely until the Prosecution's rebuttal case. And again, from the Celebici appeal judgement, it says where proposed rebuttal evidence is itself evidence probative of the guilt of the accused and where it is reasonably foreseeable by the Prosecution that some gap in the proof of guilt needs to be filled by the evidence called by it, it is appropriate -- excuse me, inappropriate to admit it in rebuttal and the Prosecution cannot call additional evidence merely because its case has been met by certain evidence to contradict it. I submit to you that that's exactly why the Prosecution sought to admit this diary, PP928, after the close of their case in chief and in rebuttal, which certainly comes after the Defence case. It was not new evidence, fresh evidence, which the Celebici Appeals Chamber went on to discuss, but it was evidence that they had long knowledge about, March 1998. They did anticipate, at least according to its theory, its usefulness. They had offered at least a portion of it in their case in chief. So if it was admissible at all, either under Rule 89 or 92 bis, it should not have come in, it was -- in rebuttal. It was not proper rebuttal evidence. On review, this Chamber should exclude the Rados diary from consideration. Something else that the Celebici Appeals Chamber focused on as to whether something qualifies as proper rebuttal evidence or not was that it does -- does the -- and I've already read a quote but they amplified on it, the Chamber amplified on it. It said that when rebuttal evidence is in fact or evidence offered in rebuttal is in fact something used to establish part of the state's case, excuse me, governments, I'm showing my origins, the Prosecution's case, then it's something that should properly be brought in their case in chief and not and rebuttal. The Trial Chamber used this Rados diary repeatedly to establish command responsibility. It was treated by the Trial Chamber as evidence of -- direct evidence of Mr. Naletilic's command responsibility and mens rea. Moving now to mistreatment of prisoners. Moving now to mistreatment of prisoners, which is ground of appeal number 17. And I'm focused on -- and that point, that ground of appeal presented the contention that evidence of torture was insufficient, and I'm going to focus on the convictions for torture under 7(1), not 7(3). The convictions on torture under 7(1) were for Fikret Begic, Witness TT, Witness B, Witness F, and Witness Z. I note first as to Fikret Begic, he did not testify at trial. There was no direct evidence as to any physical pain or the degree of physical pain and suffering suffered or the duration of it. Suggested that the evidence presented was insufficient as to torture. As to also the Trial Chamber convicted Mr. Naletilic under 7(1) of mental pain and suffering as to Fikret Begic, and I note that there is no evidence nor any findings regarding the degree or duration of the suffering of Mr. Begic. The same applies with Witness T. Also Mr. Naletilic was convicted under 7(1) of inflicting severe mental pain and suffering to and on Witness TT, and even as to him, even as to Witness TT, who did testify, there is no evidence of any lasting harm. The conviction for torture under 7(1) that I find most troubling is as to Witness B. Witness B was a young man. The evidence was that he was asked some questions and there was a pistol on a desk, but I submit to you that that's -- even if true, that does not torture make. Torture, even from -- the jurisprudence of this Tribunal and from all historical documents leading to the Statute of this Tribunal, torture is the worst of the worst. And Witness B, in what he testified to, simply did not bring the Prosecution there. As to Witness FF, he testified that he was struck three times and Mr. Naletilic ordered him to stop. No evidence of degree of harm, no evidence of duration of harm, as to Witness FF, evidence of torture, insufficient. Similarly as to Witness Z, just no evidence of duration, no evidence of degree. The vagueness of the indictment, ground of appeal number 12, and also the Chamber had asked us to address more fully vagueness of the indictment with respect to the Ljubuski prison allegations. The indictment -- I'll begin first with the Mostar events, the Mostar events, those being the allegations of forcible transfers alleged in Count 18, do not -- what was alleged in Count 18, paragraph 54, did not give sufficient notice that Mr. Naletilic was going to have to defend against transfers under 7(3) -- that his -- that responsibility was going to be attributed to him under 7(3) for transfers occurring on June 13 and 14 and September 29, 1993. What the actual -- what the actual language of the indictment said was that Mladen Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic were responsible for and ordered the forcible transfer of Bosnian Muslim civilians that started on May 9 and continued at least -- until at least January 1994. Skipping ahead, it was alleged that two large waves of forcible transfers took place in May and July 1993. No where does it say which ATG units were responsible for what transfers. No where does it say on what date was Mr. Naletilic either responsible under either 7(1) or 7(3). This Chamber in particular is well aware of the general requirements for indictments set out in the Blaskic appeal judgement. I won't trouble you with those. This Chamber certainly is well aware of it. The -- I make special note that the allegation was that forcible transfers -- two large waves of forcible transfers took place in May and -- excuse me, July 1993. There were four key episodes dealt with by the trial judgement. Dealing with forcible transfers from Mostar: May 9, May 25, June 13/14, and September 29, 1993. Mr. Naletilic was acquitted of the May events. And here is where I'm getting to perhaps the harm in the particular allegations, that we were focused, the Defence would have been focused on May and July, saying that those were two particularly large waves of transfers occurred, you'll note that from the evidence presented, Mr. Naletilic was acquitted of the May events, there was no evidence presented on any July events, the events that he's convicted of are mentioned, if they are at all, in the broad stroke that evictions took place between May and January, May 1993 and January 1994. That's not sufficient notice. It wasn't sufficient notice to trigger the possibility of conviction for events which occurred June 13/14, 1993 and September 29, 1993. I perhaps -- it does me no harm to concede that if he had been convicted of the May problems then there would have been sufficient notice, given the fact that they said there were large waves in May. But that's not what we are dealing with here. We are dealing with June and September which are beyond any sort of specificity provided by paragraph 54 of the indictment. Moving now to the vagueness of the indictment with respect to Ljubuski prison, a point which are we raise at paragraph 176 in our brief. The indictment suffers from -- it's similarly defective as to allegations regarding Ljubuski prison. What was alleged, and you have to put two paragraphs of the indictment together to decipher it, but the allegation was that beginning -- and this is paragraph 54 of the indictment, that beginning in May of 1993, going through January 1994, that -- now this is paragraph 50, that beatings and tortures were also inflicted at other detention centres and camps under the authority of the HVO, not KB, under the authority of the HVO, such as the Ljubuski prison and the Heliodrom. The Blaskic appeal judgement said that -- and I'm paraphrasing, that if -- one requirement, one of many requirements in alleging 7(3) liability is that you show -- the Prosecution show who was under control of the accused. They are talking about prisons under the control of the HVO, not prisons under the control of the KB. That does not convey how Mr. Naletilic was responsible under 7(3). I'm talking about 7(3) only because he was not found guilty under 7(1) for events at Ljubuski prison. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. But from the indictment it is impossible to decipher at what point throughout that broad period of time, May 1993 to January 1994, the Prosecution was contending that he was responsible under 7(1) or under 7(3), and as to 7(3) who he was in charge of at the time, any crimes were committed by any alleged subordinates. Reflecting on what we now know about Ljubuski prison, that is that the trial judgement was wrong when it identified Ivica Kraljevic as warden during all relevant periods. Knowing what we know now, if the Prosecution had made some allegation that the Ljubuski prison was under the control of a KB member, we might not even be here at all talking about convictions for Ljubuski prison. What the Blaskic appeal judgement talked about was that the Prosecution -- the Prosecution should not be allowed to develop its case as the trial proceeds, that notice is notice is notice, that the indictment defines what the evidence can be, what is admissible, what is relevant, and it defines what an accused may be convicted of. They did not accuse, I say they, the Prosecution did not accuse Mr. Naletilic with any degree of specificity for being in control of Ljubuski prison in any way, nor do they accuse him of being specifically responsible for those who may have committed any crimes within Ljubuski prison. I'm certain I'll have more to answer when the -- after the Prosecution's reply. I have tried to be concise and direct with my portion of my presentation now. I will make one brief comment now about sentence but I would expect to come back to that at the end. May I have one moment, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: I just make this observation, and I apologise to my colleague, Mr. Kerns, it's based on information that he has shared with me. I provide this to the Chamber as something to -- as food for thought, if you like. As of I believe February of this year, there have been something like 53 individuals convicted and sentenced by the Tribunal. Of those 53, no more than from -- of that number, no more than ten have received a sentence greater than 20 years, the sentence which Mr. Naletilic received. I believe that the number is something like five or six who have received an equivalent sentence. Based upon the evidence, based upon even the findings of the Trial Chamber, which certainly we have disputes about, but even on the findings of the Trial Chamber, placing the conduct found by the Trial Chamber along a continuum of the convictions and sentences meted out by this Tribunal, 20 years is not in step, that, as I said in my opening remarks, a sentence of no more than eight years is appropriate and I suggest perhaps even less, depending on how the Chamber reviews some of our challenges. With that, I submit the floor to Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hennessy. Mr. Meek, please. Sorry, before Mr. Meek starts, Judge Guney would like to raise a question. Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. [Interpretation] Mr. Hennessy, you stated that your client was the overall commander and he had a lot of charisma but he was not an operational commander. That's what you said. As a result, there was no reason for him to know what had happened in other locations. Is that true? Is that the case? You repeated that, it seems to me, several times throughout your submissions. Therefore, I would like to know what is your point of view, your vision, of the relationship between the operational commander and the overall commander, because there are ways of submitting reports from the operational commander, and there are ways for the overall commander to receive appropriate information relating to what is happening around in his area of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: The way I can think best to respond to that is in my sense of saying, my interpretation of the evidence, is that at best, at best, Mr. Naletilic could be viewed as a -- as we've already talked about as a charismatic figure in relation to the KB perhaps, even drawing recruits to the KB though he were not an operational commander of it. Number 1. Number 2, that perhaps, and I -- perhaps the evidence also supports that some operational commanders may have had discussions with Mr. Naletilic. That sort of relationship, that they knew each other or maybe even had discussions of events, is different than being an operational commander or being a commander as to events on the ground. So how best to answer your question? I'd say that his connection to what actually happened, and let's even make this assumption from the evidence. Let's assume that he had the type of influence, the type of authority, the type of power, where, if he had known he could have prevented a crime from happening or if he had known or had reason to know, he could have punished it after the fact, because he was not operational commander, he was not in a position to know or have reason to know before anything had happened, or even after it took place. He was not in a chain of command where reports should have been coming to him as they would to an operational commander. So he certainly was the founder of the KB. He certainly was the life-blood of it for a period of time but then that torch passed by the time of this conflict. Have I -- is there anything more, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So according to your interpretation, the overall commander has no way of knowing anything before or after the events? He has no way of knowing what is going on within the area of responsibility of the operational commander. Is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Direct response to your question is, if an overall commander truly is an overall commander, then, yes, I would say that he should know or have reason to know. But I'm not saying that -- our position here is that Mr. Naletilic was not that type of overall commander. This was not a well-defined, ordinarily established perfect chain of command where you have Mladen Naletilic, deputies and people below, and reports went up, reports went up and orders went down. We don't have that. Things were not that organised. So, in answer to your question, if an overall commander is truly an overall commander, then yes, I would be foolish to say that that 7(3) liability could not be attributed. But that's not what we have here. My dispute with the trial judgement is they placed the label, they placed the label of overall commander on Mr. Naletilic without sufficient supporting evidence for him to be truly an overall commander. And I just bring you back, I won't reiterate, back to the mens rea element that I've addressed in relationship to Ljubuski and Mostar. Those are indicative of the fact that he could not and did not have knowledge and he had no reason to have knowledge is indicative that he's not the type of overall commander that he was labelled by the Trial Chamber. So I hope that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE GUNEY
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HENNESSY
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hennessy. Mr. Meek, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, may it please the Appeals Chamber, just to follow up briefly with Judge Guney's question to Mr. Hennessy, a large amount I think in the record and judgement, trial judgement, even supports this, that a lot of Mr. Naletilic's charisma and -- in the area in Herzegovina that this indictment entails, grew from his actions with the HVO in 1992, when the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Muslims were fighting side by side and against the Serb aggressor in the Neretva Valley and they pushed the Serbs back out of Mostar. I think there was evidence submitted, and the trial judgement speaks of that action, and Mr. Naletilic therefore became something of a legend, the Prosecution witnesses mentioned that, that he -- other one submission that he was some sort of myth. Everybody had heard about Mr. Naletilic, Tuta. And it grew because of the June dawn operation where the HVO in July August of 1992, being composed of Muslims and Croats from Bosnia-Herzegovina expelled the Serb aggressors on that occasion. Even though that was a fact, we will address this additionally when we talk about mitigation at some point and probably not this morning. That again was a find -- facts that were in front of the Trial Chamber which were uncontested, so to speak. Yet the Trial Chamber found there were absolutely no mitigating factors whatsoever in Mr. Naletilic's case. And again we can address that later when we have sufficiently more time and we will have more time this afternoon, and I notice on the schedule that we also have an hour tomorrow in two half-hour shifts. Your Honours, may it please the Chamber, I am Chris Meek. I'm an attorney from Baxter Springs, Kansas. I had the privilege to represent Mr. Naletilic in the trial of this matter which commenced on September 10th, 2001 and was completed on the 31st of October, 2002. It is a privilege to be here today to address Your Honours on the issues which we've raised on appeal. We believe these issues to be many and we believe that they are important. As Mr. Hennessy indicated, I plan to speak about unlawful labour, which was known as the canal project in this case. I plan to speak about plunder, the issue of plunder, in Mostar, the issue of the lost Mostar court file and of course related cumulative errors of the Trial Chamber, the search warrant issue, and the testimonies of Falk Simang in particular and Ralf Mrachacz, the two German witnesses who came before this Tribunal. We believe, Your Honours, that the Trial Chamber utilised to a large extent three pieces of evidence, so to speak, two pieces of evidence which Mr. Hennessy has discussed so far, P704, the infamous I call it 704, the Convicts' Battalion list, allegedly the list that was unsigned, that was seized from the tobacco station in Siroki Brijeg, that was used extensively by the Prosecution after its admission over the objection of the Defence, based on a search warrant issue, the Rados diary, which Mr. Hennessy has discussed, and then the testimony of Falk Simang for the most part and Ralf Mrachacz to a lesser degree. As Mr. Hennessy had indicated -- some of these items, Your Honours, and a lot of them are intertwined -- excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Come back to 704 in a moment. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber found Mr. Naletilic guilty of Count 5, unlawful labour, in violation of the laws or customs of war, under Article 3 of the Statute, and this was in the context of a digging of a trench in the vicinity of Tuta's home in Siroki Brijeg, Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Trial Chamber did at paragraph 322 of the judgement correctly find that there was contradicting evidence, and the Chamber said it was not satisfied that the digging of the trench was for a private purpose, namely the construction of a water-pipe to supply the villa. The reason that's important, we agree with that, but you got to -- you have to understand that this also ties in with vagueness of the indictment. Throughout the trial of this matter and the case in chief, the Prosecution's case in chief, the witnesses who came forward to testify concerning this canal project all testified that they were told that it was being dug as a water supply for Tuta's house or villa, as it was defined. Another witness, I think NH, or NI, finally defined Tuta's house, said it was about a normal house, and half the homes in Siroki Brijeg were larger and nicer. It wasn't a villa but irrelevant. The point being is that during the trial and the vagueness of the indictment we were never sure what we were being charged with. In the indictment, we were charged with having used detainees to construct a swimming pool at Tuta's villa. The Trial Chamber correctly found Tuta not guilty found -- found that in fact the swimming pool they were talking about was a city swimming pool in Siroki Brijeg. It wasn't even a swimming pool located on my client's property. Your Honours, in regards to Count 5, unlawful labour, in one hand the Trial Chamber says there is contradicting evidence and it nonetheless found him guilty under Article 7(3) as being a superior and it relied on the testimony primarily of two witnesses, CC and DD. And by -- from those two witnesses, the Trial Chamber indicated it was satisfied that Mladen Naletilic knew or had reason to know that the detainees were subjected to conditions susceptible to render the labour unlawful. Now, at paragraph 325 the Trial Chamber found that the conditions of labour constituted a sufficiently serious violation of the rule of humanitarian law to fall within the ambit of Article 3 of the Statute. Again, we submit that this was based solely upon the testimonies of witnesses CC and DD. And if you look at that testimony from those witnesses and all the other evidence concerning what I call the canal project, the unlawful labour conviction, there was no evidence of any direct involvement or direct criminal liability under Article 7(1) by Mr. Naletilic. They found that he had visited the construction site on several occasions and had been seen talking to the guards while the prisoners were working. That's at para 326 of the trial judgement. Your Honour, a close review of the evidence relied upon to make this finding is that the Trial Chamber ignored, without any explanation whatsoever, the evidence that it heard from Defence witnesses NH and NI. In short, Judge, Your Honours, they -- the Trial Chamber has found Mr. Naletilic guilty under 7(3) merely because the home where he lived in Siroki Brijeg, unfortunately for Mr. Naletilic, happened to be within 400 to 500 metres from where this trench was being dug. The confusion in the Prosecution's case was that everyone was setting forth that this was a trench being dug up the hill by using this detainees as labourers to put water into Tuta's home. Well, we finally found out, no, that's not right and the Trial Chamber so found. But NH and NI, both testified. NI specifically was an interpreter, was asked by the municipality and the first Brigade of the -- 1st Brigade of the Siroki Brijeg Brigade, which was a volunteer unit in Siroki Brijeg, because he was an interpreter also, so they asked him would you please go ask some of the detainees and speak with them at the tobacco station to determine whether or not they would mind volunteering to join in some action in digging a certain canal or trench. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. NI was a home guard and he testified that he, along with three others, were there to prevent any kind of maltreating of the detainees. Of course, NI testified there was no maltreatment. He testified that none of them were forced to work, normally ten to 15 would go per day. It's about a six-week time period when NI was watching the detainees. They would go in the morning, they would take a break during the day, come back in the afternoon, they were digging, removing material, cutting surrounding bushes. NI testified that they had food, it was common military food that the soldiers, HVO soldiers ate. It came from the military kitchen where it was prepared. During the work, the detainees regularly received cigarettes, sometimes even beer. He did say it was very hot. And people usually work in that manner by taking a little time off during the middle of the day. Now, there was also testimony that -- from Witness NI that from the location where the work was starting, there is no chance to see anybody's house, let alone Mr. Naletilic's house. Could we go into closed session for just a moment? Private session, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Yes, we can go in private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours. Briefly again on the canal project, Witness NH testified that in the summer of '73, he knew and had some indirect relationship or knowledge of Sir Martin Garrod who was with the British battalion in Herzegovina at that time. He indicated that he and Mr. Martin Garrod had been talking, and he asked Martin Garrod about what to do with certain detainees, what could you do with them, instead of having them sit around all day. The testimony was that Sir Martin Garrod, who was also a Prosecution witness in this case, indicated to him that that would be good, that it would give people something to do in order to make their day go quickly, as long as you don't jeopardise their human rights. Garrod told this witness that they could not be forced to work but they could work if they wanted to work. This witness reconfirmed that the detainees did want to work, also testified that they had bigger rations of meals and other things. Your Honour, Witness BB, as set out in footnote 873 of the judgement, we submit that no reasonable tribunal of fact, no reasonable finder of fact, could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt that Tuta was guilty under Article 7(3) for any labour, for two reasons. One, all of these witnesses basically just testified, well, we were forced to work, the Trial Chamber found that that sort of work isn't necessarily illegal. However, because of the arduous conditions, the work was unlawful. We believe, Your Honours, that all these witnesses basically testified, took us to work about 8.00, we came home about 5.00, they fed us, and it was pretty hot. It was the summer-time in Bosnia. It was hot. That was the extent of it. Now, assuming, arguendo, assuming without admitting, that this is -- rises to the level of the seriousness for a war crimes charge, then what we want to know is where is the evidence that Mr. Naletilic would have specific information about the conditions or that any of his subordinates were forcing this labour. The home guards of the Siroki Brijeg Battalion and the municipality were the ones who organised the labour - and it's in the record - not the Convicts' Battalion. And, again, assuming arguendo that Mr. Naletilic was some overall commander, or had any effective control, we believe, Your Honour, and the reason that no reasonable finder of fact could find guilt beyond a reasonable doubt and to uphold this conviction would be a miscarriage of justice is because the record is devoid of any evidence that Mr. Naletilic was ever put on notice, other than the fact of the testimony of BB or DD that says we were at the bus, we were getting-- we were leaving that day, we saw the bus -- I saw the bus driver talking to Mr. Naletilic about 15 metres away, didn't hear what they were talking about. Another, CC, testified that he'd see Tuta one or two times - this is in a six-week period - close to the work site. DD we believe embellished his testimony concerning the one time he saw Tuta, because in his first statement you'll see that he said Tuta was in civilian clothes. That it was in 1996. After the Office of the Prosecutor started questioning him, all of a sudden -- or when he came to court Tuta was in a military uniform on the one occasion. So his testimony is embellished, couldn't be believed. But what the Trial Chamber has done has inferred, has just inferred, that Tuta had knowledge of what was going on. Now, just because you see Tuta around the work site is irrelevant. Any citizen in Siroki Brijeg might be by the work site or where the detainees were working on any given day. What could Tuta have known to make him guilty under 7(3)? Is there any evidence that Mr. Naletilic knew the hours of the labour? No. Is there any evidence that he knew the extent of the labour, what they were making them do? No. Is there any evidence that Mr. Naletilic knew the amount of the food that was given to the detainees when they were working? No. Is there any evidence that Mr. Naletilic knew whether they had volunteered to work or were forced to work? No. The only thing really that Mr. Naletilic could know, assuming you believe, assuming you take for granted that these witnesses told the truth, DD, CC, BB, well, Mr. Naletilic, when he saw the detainees getting ready to get on the bus that one day, well, he would know one thing. I guess he would know that the temperature was either hot or cold that day. That's basically all he would know. Everything else the Trial Chamber did to find him guilty of 7(3) is that they just imputed it. Your Honour, this goes over and over. In this case, we will talk about it more. The Trial Chamber, we submit, took our -- when they got to the guilt phase, after the 98 bis motion, when they got to the guilt phase, was he guilty beyond a reasonable doubt or not, the Trial Chamber over and over and over, adduced the evidence in a light most favourable to the Prosecution, when in fact we believe the proper legal standard is that that guilt phase, the trier of fact must find in any conflicting evidence situation, all evidence must be viewed in a light most favourable to the accused, which they didn't do. In sum - I know we are getting ready to break, Your Honours - they misapplied the fact that this would be -- this is even a -- there was a serious nature to this work, and there was absolutely no evidence that Tuta was in a position to have effective control over those folks or even know what was going on, other than the fact of the one incident or two incidents where they claim they saw him and he would know what the temperature was. But all the rest, the record is devoid of it, and the trial judgement made a leap of faith, once again, to get to a point to find him guilty under 7(3). Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Meek. Any questions from my colleagues? No. Well, if it's not the case, I think it's the right moment to break. We reconvene at 10.20, in 30 minutes. Sorry, 11.20. I'm not looking well at the clock. I'm very sorry. We will adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We will now continuing the hearing on Naletilic appeal, with the response by the Prosecution. The Prosecution will have one hour and 30 minutes for their response.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: May it please the Court, during the break my client wanted to make a request so that the Appeals Chamber could consider it between now and tomorrow. He's been allotted 15 minutes in which to make a statement, and he's indicated that he would like to have a little more than 15 minutes, if that's possible, and he indicates that he believes Mr. Martinovic will only use about seven minutes. But in any event, I'm just bringing that up. My client requested I pass that on to the Appeals Chamber to ask if it's possible if he have approximately 25 minutes to 30 minutes tomorrow. Thank you. And I would also say that due to the time period that I was able to speak, there are still issues I'll talk about, but I'll do that this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: The Appeals Chamber will consider that when we give the schedule for tomorrow. Mr. Kremer, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, firstly in response to Mr. Meek's comment about continuing his argument this afternoon, I have a problem with that, and I would hope Your Honours have a problem with that from the point of view that it doesn't allow me an opportunity to respond to issues that should have been raised in his remarks this morning. I would hope that the reply that is permitted would be a reply to any new issues that I've raised in my responses. Dealing with the command responsibility that Mr. Meek raised this morning, and I can indicate that I will be dealing with command responsibility, mens rea, the search warrant issue, the vagueness of the indictment, and Mr. Wirth will be dealing with the Rados diary, the Simang testimony, mistreatment of prisoners and forced labour. In terms of command responsibility, it is our position that there was ample evidence before the Trial Chamber to support the finding that Naletilic was the true commander and effective commander of the Convicts' Battalion. The Trial Chamber judgement starts talking about the Convicts' Battalion at paragraph 82 and continues on through to and including paragraph 175; and paragraphs 160 to 163 deal with Mr. Martinovic's role in the command structure and in respect to the Vinko Skrobo ATG subunit of the Convicts' Battalion. The difference between operative commander and overall commander that Mr. Hennessy referred to this morning at the commencement of his remarks, I think was taken out of context because he refers to the words operative commander, in 96 where in the second sentence the Trial Chamber talks about Ivan Andabak taking over as operative commander of the KB Siroki Brijeg, and operative commander of that unit does not imply and should not be taken to imply that the operative command of that unit was not held by Mr. Andabak. What is important is that the Defence witnesses suggest that another person was also the operative commander in addition to Mr. Andabak at Siroki Brijeg but the overall commander of the Convicts' Battalion, Mr. Naletilic, had his office at the tobacco station at -- in Siroki Brijeg. But, in terms of the evidence itself, you will see that the footnotes from 207 to 491 amply detail the evidence that relates to the finding that the Convicts' Battalion was controlled by Mladen Naletilic and that he was the overall commander and true commander for both operational purposes and in situations involving the carrying out of actions against various places in the Mostar region. In terms of command responsibility, the Appellant submits that if one were to examine the record, one would have doubt about the command responsibility finding because it was based solely on or primarily on Exhibit 704, the list of members of the KB in November of 1993, the testimony of Falk Simang, and the Rados diary, which is Exhibit 928. The examination of the Trial Chamber's judgement in the paragraphs listed, 92 through 175, shows that this is not accurate. That there is a misunderstanding as to the weight placed on these documents and, in fact, the testimony is full of witnesses other than Falk Simang who testified as to the command responsibility held and exercised by Mr. Naletilic, the transcript is -- and the record is complete -- or is full of documents which confirm the command responsibility held and exercised by Mr. Naletilic. And if one carefully examines the footnotes relating to Exhibit 704, the Trial Chamber did not use those references to the pay list of November to confirm that the people were members of the Convicts' Battalion before that date. They used the reference to confirm that they were still members of the Convicts' Battalion on that date. They used other evidence, witness testimony, and other evidence, to confirm that these people were members of the Convicts' Battalion at the time that the crimes were committed. And that is clear when one examines the footnotes as to the units of the Convicts' Battalion, in particular the references to the various individuals that start at footnote -- at paragraph 96 and go on through to and including paragraph 115. The footnotes include references to witnesses, to documents, and to occasionally the salary list confirming that the person was still a member of the unit in November of 1993. So a careful analysis of the Trial Chamber judgement belies the submission made by the Appellant that the Trial Chamber misused Exhibit 704 in order to find membership when the crimes were committed. In fact, that is not the case. It used it to confirm the evidence of the witnesses that testified plainly that the members of the KB committed the crimes, including Mr. Naletilic, and used the document to confirm that they were in fact members still by November of 1994. It also confirms the structure of the unit in November of 1994, which is consistent with the structure of the unit according to the testimony of the various witnesses who testified as to their contact with it. In terms of command responsibility, an independent witness mentioned this morning by Mr. Meek, Sir Martin Garrod, testified as to the command responsibility of Mr. Naletilic. His evidence is clear that when Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he met Mr. Naletilic, he introduced himself as the commander and, in fact, had the impression that he was in charge of the Convicts' Battalion. In fact, he was told he had charge of the Convicts' Battalion and was the impression that he had significant responsibility in the region. In terms of the Rados diary, if you look at the footnotes that relate to the structure of the Convicts' Battalion, the Rados diary has very little significance at all to determining the structure of the battalion, the membership in the battalion, and the command responsibility of Mr. Naletilic. In fact, the Rados diary is supportive of the evidence of all of the witnesses, and its usefulness by the Trial Chamber was for the purpose of confirming the testimony and, in fact, filling in some details of what transpired between certain events that the witnesses hadn't testified to, but those details are not significant in terms of the findings underlying the convictions. In respect of Falk Simang, again, an examination of the testimony of Falk Simang will demonstrate that he was a credible witness, and my colleague, Mr. Wirth, will speak about that. I just want to say that in an analysis of the -- in an analysis of the footnotes that make reference to the command responsibility, Falk Simang does not figure significantly in those footnotes. The testimony of other witnesses was referred to. And generally speaking, when one looks at the footnotes, Falk Simang is one of the many witnesses who was testifying as to the same event. So that there is substantial evidence confirming the evidence of the crime, and Falk Simang generally is a witness who is supportive as an insider of what actually took place at the various events. The question relating to question five, dealing with the command responsibility for Sovici/Doljani, suggests that the role of responsibility of the HVO brigades, Herceg Stjepan, is not a significant factor in determining Naletilic's role with regard to the various troops deployed for the purposes of the Sovici/Doljani operation. Our position is that the evidence is overwhelming, particularly the documentary evidence, that the finding by the Trial Chamber that Mr. Naletilic was responsible for the Sovici/Doljani incident is clear and unequivocal. I will refer you briefly to some of the documents, and many of the documents are referred to by the Trial Chamber in support of its conclusions. As early as April 15th, 1993, three days before the Sovici action, Exhibit number P299.1, an order states: "Pursuant to the agreement with commander of the southwest zone of the HZ community, Brigadier Mico Lasic, with coordinator of Herceg-Bosna, Mladen Naletilic, Tuta, with representatives of the Main Staff, Colonel Ivan Andabak, I issue hereby the following order," and then it directs a certain reconnaissance team and platoon to be at a location in Sovici on April 15th, 1993. So it is clear that he is involved in the attack, and it becomes clear with the next report that is going to the forward command post, that one was to the HVO Brigade Kralj Tomislav, and this is Exhibit P301.1, it details the preliminary steps for the Sovici/Doljani raid. And item number 7 on page 2 talks about coordinating with Tuta is being done through the Posusje unit in the Sovicka Vrata. More telling, however, is the document referred to by the Trial Chamber at paragraph 130 of the trial judgement, and this is a confidential document that is quoted, which shows that the person -- the offensive is being directed by a person of substantial political, economic and military influence, someone who is tired of signatures and political treaties, hence he has no wish to uphold the cease-fire agreement struck between the ABiH and the HVO. This person is known as Tuta and has chosen two collaborators he had with him in Operation Bura, namely Ivan Andabak and Brigadier Lasic. Now, on May 7th, a report is sent to the Herceg Stjepan Brigade which comments about the events relating to Sovici, and the author of the report, Blaz Azinovic, says in the middle of P368: "By order of Vlado Curic, Mr. Tuta's commissioner, the transport of prisoners of Sovicka Vrata, together with civilians (women and children), began around 1600 hours on May 5th, 1993. From there, in the presence of Mr. Vlado, they were taken to Gornji Vakuf under guard by buses which were waiting for them there." Next paragraph, and this is the important one: "Throughout the operations," and he's talking about earlier in his memorandum you will see April 17th and April 19th, "the conduct of our army was fair and careful so that we did not have any wounded or dead soldiers," and here is the important sentence, "Mr. Tuta commanded the overall operation in this area, Risovac, Sovici and Doljani, in which troops from elsewhere also took place such as, for instance, the Convicts' Battalion the Poskok Viper Battalion, the Grdani, the Posusje mortarmen and others whom I do not know very well." That's found in paragraph 129. And that's documents illustrate quite plainly that Mr. Naletilic had command responsibility as the Trial Chamber found for the Sovici operation and the witnesses also confirm that. You can look at the testimony of Witness E at page 4513. You can look at the testimony of Mr. Mrachacz at page 2698, confirming that Mr. Tuta ran the meetings, or used his deputies, that the orders to use the Bofors came from page -- from Tuta on page 2729. And also the Witness RR, when talking about the Sovici raid: "I knew that Tuta was attacking us because Dzemal Ovnovic had said that Tuta had called him to surrender and we were captured. They said that they had to return us over to Tuta." And that's found at page 2730. There are other documents, and I'll just list them which all confirm that Mr. Naletilic was the commander of the Convicts' Battalion and the ATG groups. Exhibit 418, which is an order issued by Mr. Naletilic, authorising Stipo Polo to have authority to control and prevent all criminal activities in the areas of Doljani, Sovici, Risovac and Vrata Cvrsnice and the right to arrest and liquidate them, as written. And special attention should be given to theft of lumber and cattle rustling. If Mr. Naletilic didn't have control, then this document has no meaning. There are other documents. Exhibit P474. Exhibit 470, which is a report which suggests that Tuta's men are involved in a particular combat action. Exhibit 548, in July of 1993, where Bruno Stojic, the chief of the department of Defence for the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina is commending a variety of groups for their courage, combat readiness and morale shown in the successful battles of Gornji Vakuf and around Gornji Vakuf. "I hereby publicly commend the Convicts' Battalion headed by Tuta." There is no doubt that Mr. Naletilic was in fact the commander of the Convicts' Battalion at all of the material times in the indictment. Finally, Exhibit 611, another commendation "for extraordinary valour and combat skill displayed during the combat in Rastani and in the fighting for the Mostar hydroelectric plant, I hereby cite the Convicts' Battalion and its commander, Tuta." Exhibit 602 is supportive of the fact that Tuta's forces are to be involved in attacks in the Mostar area and that they have a specific role to play. The documents clearly show that there is a wealth of evidence that the command responsibility, the overall command responsibility, for the Convicts' Battalion and the ATGs fell under Mr. Naletilic and the basis for the inferences to be drawn from his command responsibility in respect of the 7(3) counts is to be taken from those facts and from the testimony of the witnesses. Now, this morning, Mr. Hennessy spoke about the lack of knowledge of what was going on in the area of the Ljubuski prison and in Mostar, and in particular the beatings that were taking place there. I just want to point out that the context for knowledge and responsibility that first finds its way into the judgement, at - excuse me - I believe it's 428, which is the paragraph complained about. Yes, 428, the basis of knowledge being the transport of the prisoners from Sovici to Ljubuski prison. The knowledge of Mr. Naletilic about the conduct and treatment of his men flows not only from the incident with the bus. The incident with the bus, you will remember, is an incident where prisoners were being beaten while the bus is broken down. Mr. Naletilic encounters the bus having been pulled out of the ditch. He is -- tells his men to stop and then they proceed on.
