One can say that may be ambiguous or ambivalent in terms of its impact but the very next day at the fish farm on April 20th at noon, Mr. Naletilic sets an example for his men that continues throughout the conflict by personally beating prisoners at the fish farm and being present and observing his men beat prisoners at the fish farm, and that conduct set the stage for the continuous treatment -- mistreatment by the members of the Convicts' Battalion at various places through -- in detention facilities under the control and command of Mr. Naletilic. It is not simply one incident. It is the series of incidents that took place. I can point you to the fish farm incident; that's paragraph 353 to 369. From his active and passive encouragement of brutality by his men at the fish farm. The Mostar incident on May the 10th, paragraphs 374 through 379 where Mr. Naletilic beat someone up on the streets of Mostar in front of his men and then his men start the beating. This kind of culture that he instilled in his men clearly carried over. And he can't all of a sudden say, You have to show me that I knew of a specific beating that was going to happen, when he instilled this culture in his men that random brutality of prisoners and other people was okay and tolerated. You will not be punished for it. It goes on to the tobacco station in the summer of 1993, paragraphs 406 to 413, and the Heliodrom throughout the entire period, 429 to 436. All of these examples show that he is personally beating people, he is observing the beatings of people, he has become informed about the beatings of people, yet he does nothing to stop it. And the evidence is overwhelming that he knew or ought to have known that his men were engaged in this kind of beating and that the convictions for the beatings and the tortures on a mens rea basis cannot be disturbed because the evidence, I would submitted, is overwhelming. One can look at all of the conduct, all of the messages that are being sent to his men in support of the Trial Chamber's conclusions, and the Trial Chamber did a very good job of analysing the evidence and making those determinations. I'll just deal quickly with the search warrant question. Our position is very simply that the search warrant is a valid search warrant, that -- I'm sorry, the -- that the decisions relating to the search warrant were properly made, in terms of not permitting the Defence to go behind the search warrant and challenge it. The safeguard for the trial was that the Trial Chamber itself looked at not only the search warrant but the background documents and made the determination that they were not relevant and were not of assistance. There was an extensive procedural history relating to the attack on the search warrant that is found in our brief and I won't repeat it here. I will go specifically to the question that is raised by the Chamber relating to the question and that is whether the lack of cooperation with the state authorities was relevant. Our position is that there is no requirement by the Prosecution to cooperate with local authorities in the execution of a search warrant. It's the other way. The local authorities have the requirement to cooperate with the Prosecution in the investigation of these matters. There is a standing issue that was raised in our brief. I will not talk about it because there is some indication in the Tadic decision that perhaps standing for a narrow point like this may be permissible, even though Tadic was decided on a different basis. There is no customary international law cited by my friends opposite that suggest or establish that cooperation with local governments is required. The -- it is clear that there is no evidence on the record of a complaint by Bosnia-Herzegovina in respect of the actions taken by the Prosecution in exercising the search warrant in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Chamber made a specific finding in the suppression decision that there was insufficient evidence to demonstrate an excessive use of force and consequently, they did not permit the results of the search warrant to be excluded. What happened as a result of the admission of the evidence was that PP704, the salary list, was admitted and that I believe is the connection between the attack on the search warrant and the attack on the documents, and our position is that PP704 was a relevant document, was properly submitted, and properly admitted, and there is no basis upon which the search warrant should be found to be invalid and that the -- there was no unfairness to the -- to the Appellant in terms of its admission. Just dealing with the - excuse me for a second - indictment issue, the question has been raised about the vagueness of the indictment. Our position very simply is that the indictment was not vague. The indictment was sufficient in respect of Naletilic to properly inform him of the offences that he had to meet. The allegations against him were 7(3) allegations. The allegations required that he know -- or they set out for him the offences with which he had been charged and the facts that he had to confront. In terms of the Count 18, the forcible transfer count, the -- there are between dates May 9th, 1993 and January 1994. The offence is forcible transfer of Muslim civilians. The places specified and with respect to the beatings, as well, the between dates who committed the beatings, his men, or members of the KB. And where did the beatings take place? In various locations in and around Mostar. The beatings and tortures were committed at different bases of the KB in Mostar, Listica, Siroki Brijeg, Ljubuski. Beatings and tortures were also inflicted at other detention centres. Our response is that the procedural history, the objection to the indictment, the appeal from that objection, when it was not allowed, clearly shows that the indictment was reviewed by the Trial Chamber, found to be valid. An appeal to this Court was not initiated. But to the extent that the indictment is defective and that it doesn't provide clear timely disclosure, our position is that that was done during the course of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the pre-trial process by the Prosecution, in particular, as part of the 65 ter filings which were disclosed on July 18th, 2000, in the Prosecutor's subsequent 65 ter (E) disclosure on October 11th, 2000, and the Prosecutor's amended list of witnesses pursuant to Rule 65 ter (E)(iv) disclosed on August 16th, 2001. The 65 ter lists, if you look at the June 18th, 2000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Just a moment. Judge Schomburg would like to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: You already addressed the question of the preciseness of the indictment in relation to unlawful transfer or whatever you want to call it, and you stated the area was clear, the -- from your point of view, the person who was responsible for this was clear, but what about the time? Isn't it true what Mr. Hennessy has indicated this morning, that there was only a -- it was only two waves of forcible transfer, and what about these incidents taking place the 13th and 14th of June and, in particular, in Mostar 29 September 1993? Was this covered really by the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It was between the dates alleged in the indictment. May 9 to January 1994 were the between dates where allegedly the transfers took place, and there was a particularisation that the transfers -- that there was a wave of transfers in May and another wave in July. I will point you to the 65 ter list, which dealt specifically with the witnesses who would testify in support of the Prosecution on Count 18.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: May I invite you, one point is whether a witness testifies and the other question is whether an accused is put on notice in a way that he can defend himself against an allegation, and is it really your position that when you state from X to Y, a long period of time, all events in this period of time are covered, in particular when it's a specific day like 27th -- 29 September 1993? Isn't it a kind of shifting target when a witness comes, states there was something on the 27th -- 29th September 1993, and then you say, Hmm, it's in the time frame alleged and so therefore that's enough? Is this really your position?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: It's not a shifting target, with respect. The accused is put on notice that there are forcible transfers that are taking place between a certain time frame for which he may be held accountable. There are specific time frames, there is a specific place involved, and this is a question of particulars as to exactly how many incidents there are and when those incidents took place. Those particulars can be provided in some other form. No request for particulars was made by the accused, notwithstanding that they complained to the vagueness of the indictment. But the Prosecution did provide the accused with information about the specifics of the incidents that it was relying on in support of this count. Not only did it give them the information of the witness that would testify, it also set out for the accused the facts that the witness would give in respect of that particular date and eviction or transfer and it also set out the count to which it related and the paragraphs in the indictment to which it related. And if that isn't notice of details, then in addition to that, because the witness testimony is referred to, all of these witness statements were disclosed in B/C/S form prior to the 65 ter list being filed, and so the Defence had full information as to the evidence that would be called by the Prosecution in support of its count as identified in the 65 ter list. There is no possibility for a misunderstanding as to vagueness. And in addition to that, when the witness testifies and talks about the event of June 13th and 14th, or September 29th, there is no objection from the accused saying this is an irrelevant fact; and in fact they cross-examine on it. And so there is no vagueness here, and to the extent that there is vagueness, it's corrected by subsequent disclosures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: And the 65 ter list for Mr. Naletilic solves the problem, if Judge Schomburg believes there to be a problem, solves the problem in terms of specificity and particulars in both the Counts 18 and 11 and 12 which are the ones that relate to him. I'll deal with Mr. Martinovic tomorrow. I think I will just make one brief comment on sentence and then I will pass the podium over to my colleague. In sentencing in this Tribunal, there are a number of factors that come to play. Command responsibility is a very important one. And in this particular case, the fact that Mr. Naletilic was the commander of a large group of men who he by example for a period of several months, as the evidence shows, permitted with his participation to basically terrorise prisoners, terrorise the community, result in the forcible transfer of hundreds of people, this conduct is properly punished by a sentence of 20 years. He might argue that it's excessive relative to recent sentences. I would submit that you have to take into account his leadership example, or lack of it, really. You have to take into account the wide-scale nature of the crimes that were being committed by many of his colleagues for which he has been held responsible, and the apparent lack of remorse because he is still arguing in light of the overwhelming evidence that he wasn't responsible. The evidence clearly shows that Mr. Naletilic was responsible, he had command responsibility, the crimes were committed, he was present, he committed the crimes himself, and at the end of the day, if you agree to uphold the sentence, which we submit you should, then that factor should be taken into account. Yes, he's entitled to argue on reasonable facts, but there is no reasonable fact supporting his submission that I wasn't in command. And I would submit that that fact is an important fact that should be taken into account by this Appeals Chamber in upholding the sentence. Thank you. I will answer questions if there are any.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Judge Shahabuddeen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Counsel, we have been presented, by both sides to the argument, with references to operative command and overall command, but are we not looking for some more reliable test as to whether Mr. Naletilic was in command? Should we not be looking for a norm like this, which you may criticise, as to whether or not he was -- he had effective command superiority? Isn't that what we should be looking for?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I believe the Trial Chamber used the test of effective control, made the finding based on the test that it had announced at the beginning of the judgement, which was the appropriate one. They used various terms to discuss the structure of the KB, but ultimately their finding was that Mr. Naletilic had effective control over the entire KB and all of its units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You say so. Your colleagues dispute that. We have to come to AN conclusion on that issue. Tell me this: Would you not say that you can use the expression "overall" to indicate either the degree of control being exerted, and you can also use it to refer to the extent of that control? Now, I know I'm a little opaque on that point, so let me read to you a paragraph which you cited, paragraph 129 of the judgement, which says this -- are you with me, counsel?

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. A report of a member of the HVO 3rd Mijat Tomic Battalion describes Mladen Naletilic's overall command position in the Sovici/Doljani operation thus. And here is the quote: "Mr. Tuta commanded the overall operation in this area, Risovac, Sovici and Doljani." The suggestion there being that you could use "overall" to refer either to the degree, the degree of the control being exerted or the extent of the control being exerted. That is over, in this case, the overall operation in this area, Risovac, Sovici and Doljani.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: I believe this reference has an extent reference as opposed to the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Yes. But at the end of this chapter, the Trial Chamber finds that the Trial Chamber is therefore satisfied that Mladen Naletilic played the central command role in the Sovici/Doljani operation which was part of the larger operation to take Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we will note your submission and we will come back to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KREMER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: You can continue, counsel, or your colleague.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Steffen Wirth. I will address you this morning on ground 4 of the Prosecution -- of the Defence appeal regarding Witness Falk Simang, and I will very shortly make a few notes on the issue of wilfully causing great suffering in particular with regard to Ivica Kraljevic, and then I will address you on the Rados diary. Your Honours, I start with ground 4, regarding Witness Falk Simang and the Rados diary -- sorry, about Witness Falk Simang. The Defence challenges the Trial Chamber's assessment of Witness Falk Simang on a number of instances. Each of these challenges is addressed in our response brief and there is no need for me to repeat them today. Therefore, I propose that in the first part of my submission on this ground, I will set out from a more holistic and comprehensive perspective why the Trial Chamber's assessment of Witness Falk Simang as a credible and reliable witness was not in error. In order to do that, I will set out five factors which in our submission characterise Simang's testimony. Your Honours, I was planning in a second part of my submissions to address the matters raised in the letter of the Senior Legal Officer. However, I note that we have not heard submissions on that issue from Defence counsel, and I'm not sure whether we will get those submissions. In case we get those submissions, I would ask for an opportunity to respond to these submissions once we have them. I'll turn to the five factors. Your Honours, the Trial Chamber in paragraph 26 footnote 48, found that the testimony of Falk Simang was reliable and consistent, and it is our submission that the following five factors which characterise the testimony of Falk Simang show that this assessment was not in error. The factors are as follows: First, he was there on the ground in the middle of the crimes. Second, most of his evidence was either corroborated by or corroborated -- corroborative of other evidence. Third, he did not speak the language. Fourth, he was horrible with dates. And fifth, he was candid and he would admit if there was something he didn't know. Let me address these factors in turn. First, he was there at the time in the middle of the crimes. He knew the fish farm in Doljani. He knew the Heliodrom in Mostar. He knew the ministry in Mostar from where Naletilic often issued his commands. He also knew the actors on the ground. First of all, he knew Naletilic who was known to him as General Tuta. Further, he knew Naletilic's subcommanders, Mandic and Milicevic, known to him by their nicknames, Lija and Baja. He also knew Andabak and Mario Hrkac, who was nicknamed Cikota, and he knew Zdenko Zdena who was translating for him and for others like Mrachacz. Falk Simang also had insider knowledge of what was going on. He knew, for example, that the KB retreated after the death of Cikota, he knew that Muslims were herded into the Mostar stadium, and he knew the hours when the attacks began which -- in which he was involved. Finally, Your Honours, Witness Falk Simang had an HVO identification card and that is on the record as P354.1. There can be no doubt that Simang was a valuable insider and had firsthand knowledge of the case. I turn to the second factor. Most of the evidence Falk Simang gave was corroborated by or corroborative of other evidence. The Trial Chamber noted this on several occasions. And those occasions we refer to in footnote 176 of our response brief. For example, the Trial Chamber noted in paragraph 28, footnote 54, that Simang's evidence that the KB retreated from Doljani after the death of Cikota was corroborated by an entirely different piece of evidence, and that is the Rados diary. The Trial Chamber also noted in paragraph 358 that the testimony of the victims' brutal maltreatment at the fish farm in Doljani was corroborated by Falk Simang. Simang testified that the victims were forced to crawl on the ground towards a wooden shed while being kicked and beaten. The very same testimony was given by independent witnesses, namely the victims of those beatings. And here I refer you to the judgement paragraph 354. Moreover, the Trial Chamber noted that Falk Simang's testimony that Naletilic was the overall commander was corroborative of inter alia evidence given by Ralf Mrachacz, Witness Q, Witness T, Witness Z, and Witness CC. Also the Trial Chamber found in paragraph 91 of the judgement of Falk Simang's testimony that Andabak was Naletilic's deputy is corroborated, inter alia, by Witness T, Sir Martin Garrod, and Ralf Mrachacz. Finally, the Chamber finds that Falk Simang's testimony that looting took place was corroborative of other evidence, inter alia the testimony of Witnesses U, AB, AC, CC, MG, GG, II, WW and Q. The extent of this corroboration demonstrate that the Trial Chamber was correct in finding that Simang's testimony was credible and reliable. Come to the third factor. Falk Simang did not speak the language. He knew what he saw. For example, he could see HV patches on uniforms. But apart from what he saw, he only knew what he was told by other people who could speak in German to him, like Zdenko, or Naletilic, who could speak German. This explains that Falk Simang did not know the names of HV units in Mostar but nevertheless was able to say that there were HV units in Mostar because he could identify the patches on the uniform. I turn to the fourth factor. Falk Simang was horrible with dates. He was unable to put correct dates to events, and he himself candidly stated: "I can say what happened and where it happened, but when it happened, each individual operation, I'm not so sure." And that is transcript page 3890. Similar statements can be found on 3844 and 3856. As we have set out in paragraph 417 of our response, the Trial Chamber was very aware of this factor and it dealt with it. It gave Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. careful consideration to the assessment of information about dates from Falk Simang; for example, in footnote 426. I come to the fifth and last factor. Falk Simang was candid. Apart from admitting his problems with dates, he frequently admitted that he did not know. For example, he admitted that he did not know whether a mined mosque was in fact blown up subsequently and that is at transcript page 3808. Another example is that he admitted that he did not know how prisoners at Ljubuski prison were treated. And that is transcript reference page 3838. Other references are 3809, 3812, and 3936. Falk Simang's candour is a factor which greatly contributes to the probative value of Falk Simang's evidence. In conclusion, we submit that these five factors show that the Trial Chamber's assessment of Falk Simang's evidence was not in error. He was a true insider, there was striking corroboration. What may appear as deficiencies in his evidence is due to the fact that he did not speak the language and he was horrible with dates and that was dealt with. And finally, Falk Simang was candid and he would admit if there was something he did not know. Your Honours, this concludes my submissions on the character of Falk Simang's testimony. And instead of turning to the questions in the letter of the Senior Legal Officer, I immediately move to a few short remarks to -- with regard to wilfully causing great suffering. The first remark that I would like to make in response to what we heard this morning is there is no requirement under our torture law that there is evidence led with regard to the degree of the duration of the suffering of the witness. I'll leave it at that because I think that is clear. Your Honours also asked for a submissions on the matter of Ivica Kraljevic, and our position in that regard is as follows: For the reasons set out in the Prosecution's additional evidence motion in favour of Naletilic, the Prosecution concedes that the beating of Witness Z in the Ljubuski prison was unsafe, and the judgement references are paragraphs 422 and 453. With regard to the impact on the judgement of that concession, we would note as a preliminary matter that at paragraph 4 of the additional evidence motion in favour of Naletilic, we incorrectly stated that the beating of Witness Z in Ljubuski prison was a torture conviction. In truth, it was a conviction entered under the count of wilfully causing great suffering. Now, with regard to the impact of the judgement of our concession the Prosecution submits that given the large number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the interpreters. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. With regard to the impact of the judgement, we submit that taking away one incident of mistreatment from Naletilic's conduct and given the fact that he was not only convicted for wilfully causing great suffering but also for torture and all sorts of other counts, we submit that this concession should have no impact on the sentence and no reduction is warranted in this regard. Let me turn to the last part of my submissions, grounds 6 and 8, relating to the Rados diary. In our response we answered Naletilic's challenge with regard to the Rados diary on the basis that the particular rules of admissibility of evidence in the rebuttal stage do not apply, and the reason for that submission in our response brief was that the Prosecution had requested the admission of the evidence during -- excuse me, before the rebuttal case. However, the Appeals Chamber in its Scheduling Order phrased the matter as an issue pertaining to the Prosecution's rebuttal case, and this characterisation seems also to be consistent with the characterisation of the Rados diary as a rebuttal exhibit in the Trial Chamber's decision of 9 October 2002. Our response brief still stands. However, in the following submissions, I will address the matter of the Rados diary applying the law on the admission of rebuttal evidence. I will in the course of my argument first set out that whether or not the Rados diary was correctly admitted, no prejudice resulted for Naletilic, and in the second step I will argue that, in addition, the admission of the Rados diary as rebuttal evidence was without error. I turn to the first issue, the issue of prejudice. Naletilic was not prejudiced by the admission of the Rados diary during the rebuttal case. With regard to any prejudice, the Defence submitted two arguments: First, that it was surprised by the admission of the evidence in the rebuttal phase; and second, that it could not cross-examine the author of the Rados diary. The first argument, the surprise argument, is unsustainable. The Prosecution disclosed the a copy of the Rados diary on 18 September 2000, more than two years before the admission of the diary. Further, the Rados diary had been included in the Prosecution's exhibit list. And moreover, on 7 December 2000, during the Status Conference the Prosecution warned the Defence in the following manner. Counsel for the Prosecution said: "It is possible, although we do not intend to offer the diary into evidence, it is possible that it could become of relevance at some point during the trial for whatever purpose." The transcript reference is page 395. It was therefore clear to the Defence that the Prosecution intended to use the Rados diary at trial, even if not as evidence. The Defence had every reason to thoroughly review the diary. However, the Defence received another warning on 3 June 2002. At that date the Prosecution moved for the admission of the diary, and it took more than another four months before the diary was finally admitted on 23 October 2002. It is difficult to understand how the Defence can claim that at this date, two years after it had received the Rados diary, it was surprised by this piece of evidence. However, even had the Defence seriously considered that at this time it was surprised by the admission of the Rados diary, it would have had the opportunity to request more time from the Trial Chamber at this point in time to remedy any prejudice suffered through the late admission. The fact that the Defence did not do so shows, on the one hand, that it was not surprised, and on the other hand, constitutes a waiver of the issue. I turn to the second claim regarding prejudice; namely, the argument that the Defence was unable to cross-examine the author of the diary, Alojz Rados. As a preliminary observation, it should be noted that this alleged prejudice has nothing to do with the stage of the proceedings when the diary was admitted. And also, I will later submit, that the Defence did not have any right to have Alojz Rados called. Your Honour, before I can continue with my submissions, I would ask that we quickly go into private session, if that is possible.

utterances.text: Yes. Move to private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, in conclusion we submit that no prejudice has been suffered by the Trial Chamber's admission of the Rados diary, and the appeal could be dismissed on that reason alone. However, you do not even need to consider whether Naletilic was prejudiced because the Trial Chamber, when admitting the diary, did not commit a discernible error in the exercise of its discretion. The relevant law on discretion is set on the Milosevic joinder appeal of 18 April 2002 in paragraph 5. In accordance with this law, the Prosecution will show that the Trial Chamber did not commit a reviewable error regarding, first, the applicable law, and, second, the weighing of the relevant factors. I turn to the applicable law. The Trial Chamber did not misdirect itself to the applicable law. In its decisions of 9 and 23 October 2002, it completely applied -- excuse me, it correctly applied Rule 89(C). Contrary to the Defence submissions, Rule 92 bis is not admissible -- is not applicable, excuse me. The Appeals Chamber held in the Galic interlocutory appeal of 7 June 2002 in paragraph 31: "Rule 92 bis has no effect upon hearsay material which was not prepared for the purposes of legal proceedings." The diary clearly is not a document prepared for legal proceedings, and it's our submission that, therefore, the applicable rule was Rule 89(C). The Trial Chamber also did not err with regard to the law applicable to the admission of rebuttal evidence. And that law is set out, inter alia, in paragraphs 273 and 275 of the Celebici appeals judgement. Inter alia, the Trial Chamber specifically required in its decision that "rebuttal evidence must relate to a significant issue arising directly out of Defence evidence which could not reasonably have been anticipated." And that is a literal quote or almost a literal quote of the Celebici appeals judgement, paragraph 273. And the Trial Chamber seems even to have been stricter than required under the Celebici appeals judgement requiring, as some other Trial Chambers did, that "only highly probative evidence will be admitted," and that was in the decision of 23 October 2002. We therefore submit that the Trial Chamber did not err with regard to the applicable law. And I will now turn to the Trial Chamber's weighing of the relevant factors. First, the Rados diary is highly probative evidence. It was prepared without any considerations of the present proceedings and it is completely --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Thank you for slowing down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WIRTH
utterances.text: Sorry, let me start again. The Rados diary was prepared without any consideration of the present proceedings. It is completely independent of any other evidence led during trial and it is consistent with this evidence. Moreover, it is unthinkable that the diary is a falsification. Witness NN stated that he had heard of the Rados diary from a prisoner during the war and later also in the media. Safet Idrizovic stated that he knew Rados's handwriting because he often worked with handwritten documents from Rados. The two of them worked together. Idrizovic recognised the handwriting of Exhibit 928C, the original blue-ink copy of the Rados diary, as the handwriting of Rados. Your Honours, for other reasons why the Rados diary cannot be a falsification, I would refer you to the Prosecution's filing of 15 October 2002, registry pages 5790 to 5779. In conclusion, Your Honours, there can be no doubt that the Rados diary is highly probative. I turn now to the next requirement, the requirement that rebuttal evidence must rebut Defence evidence and must be significant. The Rados diary was used by the Prosecution to rebut the credibility of three Defence witnesses; namely, witnesses NE, NW and NL. At the 98 bis stage, the Prosecution had a strong case that Naletilic was in command of the units taking part in the Sovici and Doljani operation. The Defence tried to undermine this case through the testimony of NL. NL was trying to explain Naletilic's presence in the region with completely innocent motives. NL stated that in the middle of the fighting around Sovici and Doljani Naletilic was spending the day with his children visiting his old friend, the father of NL, over Easter in his house in Risovac. NL also stated that Naletilic did not have a Motorola with him. And he never tried to show that Naletilic had no means to communicate with his soldiers. Your Honours, this evidence was directed against the Prosecution's command responsibility case, and the Prosecution successfully rebutted it by using the Rados diary to undermine the credibility of Witness NL. The Trial Chamber did not believe, as a result of that undermining, that Naletilic's motives for his presence in the region were to visit old friends, to be with his children, and they did not believe that Naletilic didn't have a Motorola to communicate with his troops. The Rados diary also shed doubt upon the general credibility of other Defence witnesses and also on Defence Witness NL. And I refer you to examples simply to transcript pages 12703 to 12704, that is for Witness NL, to 14988 for NW, and to 1138 for NE. Given the solidity of the Rados diary, the inconsistencies in the testimony of the witnesses with the Rados diary exposed that those witnesses should not always be relied upon, and indeed their testimony was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. rejected by the Trial Chamber on a number of occasions. And the Appeals Chamber will be able to confirm, to confirm this when looking, for example, at trial judgement paragraph 129, footnote 371, paragraph 525, or paragraph 88, footnote 233. In conclusion, the Prosecution submits that the Trial Chamber did not exercise its discretion erroneously when it considered that the Rados diary could rebut the credibility of these Defence witnesses. It was open to the Trial Chamber to consider that the credibility of these Defence witnesses was a significant issue which arose from the case of the Defence and that the Rados diary was appropriate rebuttal evidence. The Defence appears to also submit that nevertheless the Rados diary should not have been admitted because Alojz Rados was not available for cross-examination at trial. The Prosecution in this regard has already set out that the Defence itself demonstrated that it did not feel prejudiced by the fact that Alojz Rados was not a viva voce witness at trial. However, in any case, the Rados diary was admissible irrespective of whether Rados was available to testify to its contents. I have set out above that the rule governing the admission of the Rados diary was Rule 89(C) and not Rule 92 bis. And we set out in paragraph 454 of our brief that it is not mandatory for the admission of a document under Rule 98(C) that the accused be given the opportunity to cross-examine the author of a document. In the present case, the Prosecution took various steps to obtain Rados as a witness. Apart from investigating his whereabouts, it requested and received the help of the Trial Chamber. And the extent of our efforts is documented in the Prosecution's confidential submissions of 13 September and 15 October 2002. In any case, the witnesses through which the Prosecution finally tendered the document, in particular Witness Safet Idrizovic, provide a very sound foundation to the authenticity of the Rados diary. And another part of that same foundation is the fact that there is very -- that the Rados diary is widely corroborated by other evidence. The Prosecution submits that under these circumstances, the Trial Chamber did not err in the exercise of its discretion when it decided that the diary had evidentiary value despite the fact that its author was not available for cross-examination. Your Honours, that concludes my submissions. And obviously I'm available for questions which you may have.

I think we have talked about some of them, but just let me say that in paragraph 89 of our revised appeal brief we claim that the trial record support our submission that Falk Simang was not yet a member of the KB or Convicts' Battalion on 19th and 20th of April and that it was disbanded at the end of 1993. Seven and maybe to my mind, the most interesting and maybe important part that you ask is the details regarding Mladen Naletilic's ill health during trial and whether he raised it as a mitigating factor. utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The Defence for Vinko Martinovic intends to present their submissions in the following way. I will present our appeals brief and my colleague, Mr. Kerns, will respond to the Prosecution appeal. In this part that I consider very important, I will turn to all the three grounds of appeals, the first one is the errors of law where I will especially talk about the existence of an international armed conflict in relation to Mr. Martinovic. The second ground of appeal, errors of fact. I intend to discuss the matters, the events relating to the murder of Nenad Harmandzic and the so-called wooden rifles incident. I also intend to talk about the sentence and probably after the break, I will respond to the Judges' questions that were put to us earlier on. In relation to the first ground of appeal, errors of law, we object to two matters. First of all, the Trial Chamber erred in finding that there it was an international armed conflict in the indictment period. And second, that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that alternative charges could be brought against the accused Martinovic and cumulative convictions could be entered against him. I will talk about this today only in relation to the international armed conflict, although Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. I do stand by our submissions as contained in the appeals brief in their entirety. In relation to the existence of an international armed conflict the Defence presented two theses. First, that the existence of an international armed conflict was not proven; and second, that the accused Martinovic could not be held responsible for participating in an armed -- in an international armed conflict because he did not know, was not aware, and did not intend to participate in one such conflict. In total, the existence of such a conflict was entirely without his knowledge and awareness -- out of his knowledge and awareness. I intend to discuss this matter because I consider it very significant for the Defence as it incurs responsibilities under all the charges under Article 2. I refer to the Kordic judgement, paragraph 311, where this matter was examined from a different point of view, but the position of the Appeals Chamber was very clear in relation to the commission of the accused, that it had to be proven that the accused was aware of the contextual and background information related to the existence of an international armed conflict. I know the position of the Appeals Chamber in this particular matter related to Kordic so I will not further elaborate on that. In relation to the international armed conflict, and specifically in relation to Mr. Martinovic, we are found in a similar situation. In the relevant period of time, Martinovic did not know and was not able to know that he participated in an international armed conflict and that this circumstance was something that he was not aware of. What do we base this submission of ours on? It was only upon the receipt of the indictment that Martinovic became aware of the charges against him in terms of his having participated in an international armed conflict, which surprised him because it has been shown beyond doubt that Vinko Martinovic was a private by rank, that he commanded over the smallest military structure, a group of a dozen soldiers that, together with this group of soldiers, throughout the war, he held one and the same Defence line in Bulevar Street in Mostar, which was 100 to 150 metres long. Furthermore, Martinovic's units never moved away from this defence line. They never participated in any actions outside Mostar, and it is beyond any doubt that -- beyond any dispute that Martinovic did not participate in any military meeting. It is beyond dispute that he was not a member of any political party and did not have contacts with any high-ranking political or military figures. It is also beyond dispute that Martinovic had practically been fighting in Mostar in front of his own home, first by fighting the Serbs, and then by fighting the Muslims who attacked that part of the town. To him, this was a local conflict entailing defence. Neither he nor any of his soldiers could conceive of the fact that they participated in any international armed conflict simply because they did not have any information to that effect. That this is how the matter stands is shown by the fact that the Prosecutor, throughout the trial proceedings, never even attempted to present the situation in a different light or to show that Martinovic in any way was aware of an international armed conflict and of his participation in it. Therefore, in no part of the presentation of evidence on the part of the Prosecution was evidence adduced to that effect. Whether Martinovic had any awareness or knowledge about it was best shown by a witness who was the head of the monitoring mission in Mostar, who explained the entire situation in Mostar and, in particular, Martinovic's role in it. Witness Gerner [phoen] was put a specific question as to how he, a person who was now retired and who was in Mostar throughout the relevant period, how he saw the role of a soldier such as Vinko Martinovic under the circumstances that were known at the time with the separation line in Mostar. He said that such a soldier could only afford to think about how to keep his head on his shoulders for 24 hours a day. He could not have access to any other information or knowledge. Therefore, I believe it has been established that Martinovic did not know and could not have known about the existence of an international armed conflict and that therefore he cannot be held responsible for it. Furthermore, it is the position of the Defence that the accused cannot be charged with the existence of an international armed conflict as a fact that was established only at a later stage but which constitutes a very significant element of the criminal offence. It is the opinion of the Defence that in order for a person to be held liable for a criminal offence, he has to be aware of all the elements of the offence and has to have the intent to commit the offence. Martinovic could not have known about the existence of an international armed conflict and did not have the intent to participate in it. He was fighting in front of his home against his fellow citizens who lived across from where he lived on the other side of the street, whereas he is being charged here as an aggressor, as a person who participated in the forces of an aggressor. This has nothing to do with the evidence adduced in this case. We believe that Martinovic's subjective relation to the international armed conflict must be considered as an important element of the crimes under Article 2 of the Statute. It is our opinion that in a criminal proceeding, nobody can be held liable for criminal responsibility under those circumstances, and the very fact that in objective terms there was an international armed conflict, this does not automatically incur Martinovic's criminal responsibility. There is no strict liability in criminal law unless there is the awareness and the intent. In the absence of these, there can be no responsibility. This is our position in relation to this fact. Furthermore, in relation to the first part of the appeals brief dealing with errors of law, we have presented our objections to the alternative charging and cumulative convictions. I would like to go back to this issue in connection with the Judges' questions. I will now turn to the second ground of appeal, i.e., errors of fact, that is Counts 13 and 14, murder of Harmandzic. The central part of the judgement is the conviction of Mr. Vinko Martinovic for the murder of Nenad Harmandzic. I appeal to the Appeals Chamber to closely review our appeal in relation to these counts. There are three challenges raised by the Defence in this respect: First, that the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the documents adduced by the Defence are incorrect. Second, the Trial Chamber erred in excluding the evidence or rather in deeming the evidence of a witness, Defence witness, not credible. Third, the Trial Chamber erred in identifying the -- in finding the identification of Nenad Harmandzic as proper. These are the three errors that I will try to further elaborate on. In paragraph 503, Trial Chamber finds that Nenad Harmandzic was seen for the last time in Vinko Martinovic's unit, and it is on this basis that the Trial Chamber concludes that Nenad Harmandzic found his death in this unit. The only fact that is not in dispute from this paragraph is that Nenad Harmandzic was in Vinko Martinovic's unit. The only controversial matter is whether he was later on in the hands of a different unit. If it were to be proved that Nenad Harmandzic was subsequently held by members of a different unit, then Vinko Martinovic must be acquitted of this conviction. Throughout the trial, this is precisely what the Defence submitted, that Nenad Harmandzic had been returned to Heliodrom from Vinko Martinovic's unit, whence he was taken to a different unit and disappeared without trace. The Defence based its submissions exclusively on the documents provided by the Prosecutor. Which evidence was that specifically? The testimony of Witness AD, the closest relative of Nenad Harmandzic, stated before the Tribunal that on the 12th of July, he had seen Harmandzic in Vinko Martinovic's unit and that he had heard that subsequently he was returned to Heliodrom on the 12th of July. Now, did Harmandzic disappear without trace on the 12th of July? And is it true that he left Martinovic's unit alive? The Prosecutor provided documents which show that the next day, on the 13th of July, Nenad Harmandzic was alive and well in the detention centre of Heliodrom from where he was taken on the 13th of July to the premises of the military police unit for labour, a unit which are had nothing to do with Vinko Martinovic. The documents show that subsequently Harmandzic fled from this particular unit and disappeared without trace. Therefore, this was the Prosecution witness and the Prosecution documentation that told us the entire tale concerning Nenad Harmandzic which had an unfortunate ending in the 1st Light Assault Military Police Unit on the 13th of July. The only reasonable inference from this evidence, and I wish to reiterate that this is Prosecution evidence, is that Vinko Martinovic cannot be held responsible for the -- for murder. So how did it come that the Trial Chamber convicted Martinovic for murder? First of all, the Trial Chamber stated that the contents of these documents were incorrect. That was the first inference which we considered to be erroneous. So how did the Trial Chamber arrive at this inference? None of the witnesses stated anything to that effect. This was an inference made by the Trial Chamber on its own, by simply concluding that the documents were not correct as well as the testimony of Witness AD. The Defence wishes to defend the right of the accused to be tried on the basis of evidence and not on the basis of presumptions. We submit that the Trial Chamber could not base its inference on any piece of evidence to the effect that these documents were incorrect and base its conviction on this inference. Let us look at the erroneous inferences of which the Trial Chamber bases its conviction. Paragraph 491 of the judgement, the Trial Chamber states, in document PP454, it states that on the 13th of July, Milenko Cule, Cuke, took Harmandzic to the military police unit. The Trial Chamber assumes that Harmandzic was not taken to this unit, as stated in the document, but, rather, to Martinovic's unit. So where does this assumption come from? The Trial Chamber states that this was a common practice and that he must have been taken into a different unit. This is not true. This was not a common practice, because there were such instances where drivers would take prisoners from one unit to another, but the evidence adduced in relation to this do not show this. In paragraph 492, in relation to another exhibit, PP774, it is stated that Harmandzic fled from that unit. The Trial Chamber concludes that the documents are false in claiming this. Therefore, the Trial Chamber again concludes arbitrarily that the document contained false information. This has even been taken as a piece of evidence against Martinovic, that this document was to have been used to cover up for the entire story. [No interpretation]. Something perhaps is not wrong but I will continue. Everything is all right now. I would briefly like to speak about the assumption of the Trial Chamber that this one document, included false information, and that is why the entire document is false. That is the Trial Chamber's assumption. So where does this idea come that there was false information there? According to the Trial Chamber, the driver of Martinovic was instructed once he came to Heliodrom to falsely inform the Heliodrom staff that Harmandzic had escaped and that is the basis on which the Trial Chamber builds its theory, a construction, about how this false document came about. However, what is not quite right here? That is that in all of these documents, you have the name of Milenko Cule from the military police, and in all the parallel documents you have another person from the military police appearing in the documents. If the assumption of the Trial Chamber were correct, that now Martinovic's driver had brought false information and it would not have been possible to put in a different unit and it would not have been possible for him to be asked where is detainee Harmandzic and for him to say, well, he was with us today and he has just fled from the military police, when this assumption were to be true, then it would always have been written ultimately from which unit he had escaped. So therefore, these assumptions of the Trial Chamber, that wrong information was entered into the documents, simply cannot hold. The testimony of Witness AD is easily ignored and simply a new construction is made on this basis. The position of the Defence again is that the Trial Chamber reached on its own initiative several unfounded assumptions based on which they drew the wrong conclusion about the incorrect information from the documents which I cited and then shed a completely false light on a number of exhibits. If we remove these assumptions what are we left with? Pure objective exhibits which speak for themselves, documents where, how, and when he disappeared, and we have Prosecution Witness AD who confirmed the dates when he was returned. So if we remove the assumptions, we have the clear conclusion that Nenad Harmandzic disappeared on the 13th of July, 1993 from the military police unit and could not -- this could not be the responsibility of Martinovic. However, the Trial Chamber drew a completely different conclusion. This is only one part of the mistakes in relation to the documents. The Trial Chamber did try to explain all of their conclusions. In paragraph 507, the Chamber summarises why Martinovic is guilty. It said that he incited his soldiers to mistreat Harmandzic when he was there. He prevented Harmandzic from returning to Heliodrom. He gave false instructions to his driver that Harmandzic had fled, and he gave instructions on the burial of the body of Harmandzic and how to conceal this act. Our question -- now I'm moving to the second error by the Chamber, what is the basis of the conclusions of the Trial Chamber on the burial, the false information by the driver and so on? The basis is just the testimony of one witness, a Prosecution key witness, who testified in public and that is Halil Ajanic. All of this, therefore, is based on one testimony from which the Trial Chamber bases its conclusions and draws its picture. What kind of a witness is Halil Ajanic? The Trial Chamber Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. says this is a reliable, sincere witness who did not try to conceal his psychiatric difficulties. Psychiatric difficulties, why does the Chamber mention that? Because we had brought an expert witness here, Drazen Begic, a psychiatrist, an expert witness, and we gave him all the medical records of Witness Ajanic, and we asked Expert Begic whether this person, in this particular mental state, could be a reliable witness, and Psychiatrist Begic says this person suffers from alcoholic psychosis which implies hallucinations, all kinds of disturbed thoughts. He also suffers from amnesiac syndrome, failure of memory, bad, weak concentration, and he also suffers from debility, which is a degree of mental retardation, making him uncritical and susceptible to influence. That is as much as our expert witness psychiatrist said about this witness. What are our objections to the decisions by the Trial Chamber? The Trial Chamber rejected the expert's findings. The Trial Chamber found that it was all right for -- that -- and found that this was a sincere witness, regardless of his psychological problems. The Trial Chamber, who are lawyers, cannot reach, and in that way, eliminate expert opinions about the mental condition of a witness. According to the Trial Chamber, this psychiatrist expert witness or his findings are not meritorious but the findings of the Trial Chamber is meritorious. I do not wish to go into why the Chamber disregarded Begic's findings. The Trial Chamber stated that the -- that Dr. Begic did not examine the witness, that he came to his conclusions based on the medical documentation. He was given the diagnosis, he looked at it, he came here and gave his opinion. The Trial Chamber was of the opinion that this was just done on the basis of documents and therefore did not find it acceptable. This is our second objection, a key witness from whom all of these theories stem, who happens to be a psychologically sick person, according to us, cannot have more weight and the Trial Chamber cannot disregard an expert opinion unless there is another parallel expert witness that can be used to support its view. Another question which for us is also very important concerns another error of the Trial Chamber, and that is the verification of Nenad Harmandzic. We had a whole new situation where Nenad Harmandzic had disappeared, and now during a mass exhumation in Mostar, allegedly his body was identified on that occasion. No DNA analysis was carried out. Identification was done without DNA analysis, and the conclusion presented here to us by Dr. Zujo, a forensic expert, is that this was the body of Nenad Harmandzic. Why is this important? If this happens to be his body, then many of these stories by witnesses can fit in on whether he was with Martinovic or not. This is an important question, which is important because it can be inserted into various parts of this whole story. Very well. Zujo, this expert for -- a forensic expert said that this was the body of Nenad Harmandzic. The Defence brought before the Trial Chamber another expert, Dr. Josip Skavic, an expert who carried out the largest number of identifications in Europe because he just happened to be heading the teams in this country which had been waging war for a number of years. We called expert Skavic to double-check Dr. Zujo's findings and to say whether this identification was carried out properly or not. Skavic said there is a large mistake which was done in the identification. The identification cannot be reliable because Harmandzic was 1.92 metres tall. When we take this body and measure the length of the bones, it was established that the person in question was between 1.82 to 1.85 metres tall. So there is a difference of 16 centimetres in these calculations, and it has to be taken into account in deciding whether this was that person or not. Skavic said that such a large difference in measurement is something that indicates that it is not reliable to say that this was the same person. There is a margin of perhaps three or four centimetres that is tolerated but not one of 16 centimetres. The Defence says all right, the identification was not conducted properly. Let's put aside all of these testimonies and everything that relates to the -- that body. This is the error of the Trial Chamber that we are pointing out for the Appeals Chamber. The Trial Chamber said it's all right, what Dr. Zujo said, but it's not all right what expert Skavic said. The Defence again asks itself how the Trial Chamber can decide on an absolutely expert question such as the identification of a person, and having heard two experts with two different opinions, how can the Trial Chamber reach a meritorious decision on that? It did not meet its obligations in deciding which of the two experts was right. And this is actually the basis of all subsequent mistakes. I would like to just mention three important mistakes in this basis of appeal, wrong documents, mistaken testimony by a witness, and also testimony of expert witnesses regarding the identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I find myself a bit lost with your calculations as to the identification. You mention 1.92 metres and then between 1.82 and 1.85 and then you made a difference of 16 centimetres. Do you have the exact figures? Because --

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This is quite possible, Your Honour. I will give you the precise number. Dr. Josip Skavic, expert witness of the Defence, brought into question this identification claiming that this particular body was between 1.82 and 1.85 metres tall. Nenad Harmandzic actually, when he was alive, was 1.92 -- 1.92 centimetres tall.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 1.96, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this mistake, from 196 to 182, according to me is, let's see, oh, it's 14 centimetres. Yes, 14 centimetres. And from 1.95 to 1.96 it's 11 centimetres. That would be it. My apologies, Your Honour, for making this mistake in my calculations. I will continue. Isn't it absurd that in order to prove the killing of Harmandzic the Prosecution has to dispute its own document? In order to prove that, they have to disprove or dispute their own documents and their own witness. In that case, what did the Defence do? It just brought two experts, which were then eliminated by the Trial Chamber outside of their area of competence, and this is why we would like to have Martinovic acquitted on this count. Now I would like to move to a second incident described as the incident with the wooden rifles. That is what we refer to during the trial. These are Counts 2, 3, 4 and 5. According to this item, the Trial Chamber decided that Martinovic was guilty because on the 17th of September 1993, he was heading an offensive by the HVO in the Bulevar Street and that under his command or order, several detainees were given false wooden rifles and that they were forced to walk along a tank in order to find where the enemy positions were. In reference to this count, the Defence claimed right from the beginning that this incident actually happened in a different unit. It did happen but in a different unit, and now Martinovic is being charged with it for the simple reason because Vinko Martinovic was the only person here from Mostar on trial at that time. That event did happen but it happened in a different unit. Now, we have Vinko Martinovic in the court-room, we have an incident, and we put them together. This was something that the Defence stated at the time. Why are we saying that? Again, we take the Prosecution document. We don't have our own documents on this. According to Prosecution documents, this action on the 17th of September, it says that Vinko Martinovic did not head this action, he refused to, and it was led by a different person. In this document, PP608, the action is described that entire day what happened and so on. However, there is nothing there about war prisoners, prisoners of war. There are no tanks. There is none of this that Martinovic is being charged with. Further, in Prosecution document P601, item 1, it states that all of those persons who came, who were brought on the 17th to Martinovic were all regularly returned to the Heliodrom, and we don't have there story given to us by the Prosecutor that some of them fled, some of them were wounded and so on. Prosecution document P601.1, as well as another one, P601, as well as another one, P601.12, also says that. The Trial Chamber asks me where was it that I actually found in this document that it says that these prisoners of war were returned? I have brought this document. I checked that in the records. It's P601.1. It's a little bit difficult to find because these are log books with a lot of pages, and I will tell you this is page 01535273 entitled the 17th of September, 1993. And in reference to Vinko Martinovic's unit called Vinko Skrobo, it says, which prisoners of war were taken for labour to him, and at the end it says which ones were returned, returned on the 27th of September at 1940 hours. So they were taken to Martinovic on the 17th and were returned on the 27th of September at 1940 hours. This second document that I referred to entitled -- or with the number P55612.1 it says the prisoners were brought to Martinovic. And then it says on the 27th of September, the remaining 12 detainees were returned who had been held over for labour. I do not want to spend too much time on this. The Appeals Chamber will have the opportunity to peruse the documents. They asked for the reference, and now I have given the reference. What are we trying to say? First of all, we are saying the event did not occur in the unit. All the prisoners 245 that were brought to Martinovic were returned and the wooden rifle story was transplanted to the Vinko Martinovic unit and that is what we are stating. The Trial Chamber did not accept this. We hope that the Appeals Chamber will accept it. The Trial Chamber stated that they had witness statements --

utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Whilst you are just referring to documents, exhibits -- sorry that I only come back now to the point in relation to the alleged killing. utterances.text: [Interpretation] The document D2/14 has a different number classified as P, I don't have it here, but this document was admitted into evidence under a different number. I may perhaps look into the matter over the break and then come back to you.
