utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is a different number and I will do my best to find it. Let us go back to the wooden rifles incident. The Defence position is that the documents indicate that this incident did not take place in our unit. Now, the Prosecution says we have witness statements to that effect. And there are witnesses PP, J, OO, Q, and others, who testified as to the circumstances of this incident. In paragraph 282, the Trial Chamber states that there are large discrepancies in the witness statements themselves, and the Chamber is of the opinion that they were probably involved in a similar event which took place on that same day with the participation of prisoners. This statement came as a particular surprise to the Defence. This was a completely arbitrary inference drawn by the Trial Chamber. Nobody ever maintained that there were several such events on the same day. The Prosecutor called witnesses to testify only in relation to one event. Since the testimonies differed and allegedly all these persons took part in this incident, the Trial Chamber inferred that probably some of the witnesses referred to another such similar incident transpiring on that same day somewhere else. This is exactly what the Defence claimed, that it had happened elsewhere. To clarify further what our objections in relation to the Trial Chamber inference are, how could the Trial Chamber base such an inference that there were -- there must have been several similar incidents transpiring on the same day simply on the differing witness statements? Because some of the witnesses stated that there was another such incident. This is another error that cannot be overlooked. We do accept that there was one such incident which took place elsewhere but not that there were several such incidents as inferred by the Trial Chamber. The Prosecutor advocated such a thesis in order to patch up differing witness statements by claiming that perhaps some of them might have been elsewhere. However, we find this unacceptable and we have Prosecution documents attesting to that. Now, why do these witness testimonies differ so much? We presented matters going to the credibility of these Prosecution witnesses, that these witnesses were being prepared by the secret police. We did not simply fabricate this as a Defence team because this witness testified against us. It wasn't on this basis that we claimed that the witness was proofed by the secret service. At one point, when evidence was lacking in support of the wooden rifles, the Prosecutor appeared in court-room holding one such wooden rifle that they claimed that had been used during the incident because allegedly one of the witnesses stated that they had preserved a rifle. However, while testifying in court-room, he did not want to say how he came by the rifle and where he kept it, and that is how suddenly out of the blue a wooden rifle appeared in the court-room in support of the Prosecution submissions. That's where we mention the secret police as having come into play. Then one day, OTP expert, Apolonia Bos, came to testify in relation to this incident. She was asked about where she came by the rifle, and she replied that she had received it from representatives of the secret police and had originated from an unidentified witness. Our question at the time was why don't we call this person to whom the rifle belonged to testify in the court-room? Apolonia Bos stated that the person did not want to testify unless some of her requests were met, like relocation into a third country, different identity papers and so on. Therefore, one such testimony of a Prosecutor -- Prosecutor's expert testifies to the vagueness of the whole information. Had the Trial Chamber had the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. sensitivity to notice these details, it would have come to the right conclusion, rather than inferring that there must have been several such incidents. We contend this inference because we find it unacceptable. Therefore, in relation to the wooden rifles incident, we considered that the Trial Chamber erred significantly and that the inference and the conviction should be reversed and the accused acquitted. I have some further comments relating to Counts 2 to 8, and I would therefore like to deal with the third ground of appeal, sentencing, and then I might come back to some of these matters after the break. On the matter of the sentence, which is our third ground of appeal, we respectfully submit that the Appeals Chamber should acquit the accused on all these counts. We appeal the sentence because we believe that the Trial Chamber failed to properly evaluate the mitigating and aggravating circumstances in relation to the accused; namely, the Trial Chamber did not take into consideration as a mitigating circumstance his voluntary surrender to the Tribunal. It failed to consider as a mitigating circumstance the assistance Martinovic afforded to the captured Muslims, Muslim neighbours, and his general attitude toward members of Bosnian Muslim ethnicity. This was not considered as a mitigating circumstance. We also believe that the Trial Chamber erred in considering his command role as an aggravating circumstance. To the question whether Vinko Martinovic surrendered voluntarily to the ICTY, the Trial Chamber replied in the negative. In our opinion, voluntary surrender entails an accused's will and actions to be taken to that effect. However, what also needs to be taken into consideration are the general circumstances of the accused at the time when he learns about the indictment. Martinovic was in detention of the county court in Zagreb at the time when he learned of the indictment issued by the ICTY. Now, the question arises as to whether a person who is held in detention can voluntarily surrender to the ICTY at all. Now, the Defence, unlike the Trial Chamber's inference, is of quite the opposite opinion. A detainee is in a position to clearly express his will and take steps to facilitate his extradition to the Tribunal, just as it can express his will not to respond to the summons of the -- of a tribunal, and to hinder extradition. We have several such examples in this particular judgement at hand, two such cases were

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: of them voluntarily surrendered. Now, Vinko Martinovic clearly expressed his will to voluntarily surrender to the ICTY in The Hague by stating that he wished to be extradited to The Hague at once upon learning of the indictment against him by stating that he did not feel guilty, that he wanted to prove his innocence before this Court without procrastinating his extradition. The state attorney of the Republic of Croatia was opposed to Vinko Martinovic's extradition to The Hague and appealed before the Supreme Court in order to prevent his extradition. Vinko Martinovic also had the right to appeal the extradition decision all the more so since the state attorney of Croatia was opposed to his extradition. Now, what did Vinko Martinovic actually do? He stated that he waived his right of appeal and asked that he be extradited to The Hague as soon as possible. Therefore, under these circumstances, Vinko Martinovic clearly expressed his will to be extradited into The Hague and clearly undertook all the actions within his power to facilitate his extradition. Now, what does voluntary -- what does constitute voluntary surrender, if this does not? Therefore, another matter that is very significant in this respect. If voluntary surrender is regarded a mitigating circumstance, the purpose of which is to encourage other accused to voluntarily surrender, then it is in this context that Vinko Martinovic's example is significant because the public at large in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina followed the entire matter through the media, whether he was going to go to The Hague or not, and it was quite clear to the public that Martinovic wanted to go to The Hague without any doubt. However, this Trial Chamber found it doubtful. I think it is quite clear that this should have been considered as a mitigating circumstance in favour of the accused Martinovic. Another important mitigating circumstance that was not even considered by the Trial Chamber, namely Martinovic's attitude and assistance afforded to Muslim prisoners and neighbours during the war. The Defence called dozens of witnesses, Muslims, precisely to deny this black-and-white image that was presented of him, and I have enumerated these witnesses countless times. All of them were victims of persecution, MA -- MB and so on. We have heard what treatment he afforded them. This is beyond any dispute, and this wasn't a matter disputed by the Trial Chamber itself. The Trial Chamber simply concluded that these were privileged persons who he decided to assist, whereas he did not assist others. Now, our reasoning is, if I am to be convicted because of those who I did not assist, then I should be granted some credit for those who I did provide assistance to. I do not wish to go back into what the persons testified to, that there was a Muslim family that he concealed in the cellar of his home from the Croatian army, and their testimonies as to how he saved their lives. Unfortunately, I don't have the time to relay all these matters here. I have a question for the Judges now. I will end the sentencing matter in five minutes now, and perhaps I could be allowed to finish this before the break and then resume afterwards on other topics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence is of the opinion that there exist very important mitigating circumstances such as the assistance provided to Muslim prisoners, neighbours, some of whom testified before the Tribunal here. In our opinion, the -- all these testimonies constitute an important mitigating circumstance that has to be taken into consideration. On the issue of aggravating circumstances, the Trial Chamber erred in finding that the command role of Vinko Martinovic was an aggravating circumstance. The Defence holds that the mere fact of a person being a commander cannot be an aggravating circumstance held against him, especially if he had already been convicted under 7(3). In the case of a commander who really held command, it -- such an aggravating circumstance could hold. However, a person holding a low commanding position cannot be held responsible to the same extent as a general can. I believe that the Trial Chamber erred in finding this as an aggravating circumstance and that as such it cannot stand. Now let us compare the sentences themselves. I wish to say that the sentences passed down in the cases similar to this one prove that the sentence passed in relation to Mr. Martinovic is an unfair one. I did not wish to further elaborate on this. This can be found in our brief. Another important remark, which is a novelty in a way: In the sentencing procedure, the Trial Chamber erroneously evaluated Martinovic's role. The role as evaluated by the Trial Chamber is exaggerated and hence the sentence. Now, why are we of this opinion? At the time of the trial against Naletilic and Martinovic, they were presented as the persons who were responsible for every evil that took place in Mostar. When the sentence was passed for Martinovic and Naletilic, the Prosecutor came up with a new indictment in relation to Mostar involving six Bosnian Croats in pleading joint criminal enterprise. However, where is Martinovic in this particular indictment? Well, he's no where to be found. Had they known at the time of their trial what sort of a responsibility it all incurred they would not have been given such harsh sentences. The Prosecutor must have been preparing for this sentence for seven or eight years. Now, Martinovic was given a sentence that is unfair and unduly and disproportionately harsh. Martinovic came here to receive a fair trial and a fair sentence. And he has the same expectations in relation to the Appeals Chamber. That is the only thing he requires, a fair trial and a fair sentence. Our additional evidence that we wanted to lead in the appeals -- at the appeals stage was excluded, and I know that my client is dissatisfied because of it. However, we do have a fair trial now and now we do expect an equally fair sentence. Now, in our opinion, what sort of a sentence would that be? Well, a sentence which follows from a conviction based on allegations proved beyond any doubt, and that would be what I had to say in this part of my presentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Par. We will now break for 30 minutes. Before doing so, I would like to tell the parties that I've been informed that the redaction we made earlier in the record actually went out to the public because the point was raised too late to -- we have only 30 minutes to redact before it goes to the public. So I would like to urge the parties first to be careful in dealing with protected information, and secondly, if they notice that some protected information has been given to raise it immediately with the Bench in order that we can redact it on time. We break until five to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: So we resume now the hearing. [B/C/S on channel 4].

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not get an interpretation into Croatian. I don't know if you were getting interpretation. Perhaps we can try to translate. All right. If you understand me, that's fine, then. We can just continue. In this second part, I would like to respond to the questions that the Chamber posed. In preparing for this hearing, there were two groups of questions; one group referred to the imprecisions in the indictment that we noted in our appeal. The second group of questions sought some clarifications regarding certain points. I would like to start from the questions relating to the things that are not quite clear or indistinct points in the indictment relating to paragraphs 143, 184, 417 and 408, as well as paragraphs 431, 434, and 453 from our appeals brief. In all of these paragraphs, the Defence stated that the acts cited in these paragraphs were not contained in the indictment. Our position was that we were not charged and therefore could not respond. We were asked by the Trial Chamber whether we had later received sufficient information in order to understand what the charges were. That is at least how I understood it. I would like to respond generally to all of our objections and then perhaps return to some specific paragraphs. In relation to each paragraph where the event was not cited in the indictment, we believe that we were not charged for that particular event or incident. I will go back to the specific paragraphs I mean. Why do I think that? Why do we have this position and how did we receive this information? We are of this position because from our legal practice, from the legal schools we come from, it states that the indictment has to clearly state the charges. This is a very clear situation for the accused as well as for us. There can be no dilemmas there. When we came to this Tribunal, we understood that this wasn't quite like that, that there are some broad formulations in the indictment and that we have to be very careful about what the charges are. However, we never actually felt that each testimony by each witness can be part of the indictment. This is something that we encountered only in the judgement whereby each witness statement can be a kind of mini-indictment brought into the statement and then if that should pass, it passes. This is, as far as I'm concerned, something that I did not expect and it's something of a surprise for me. Especially in events where there are specific incidents. For example, the expulsion of the 29th of September. If I have persecutions for the 13th, the 14th, I don't know what other specific dates, perhaps that's not so important right now, I think that when we are talking about the 29th of September, then I'm not charged for that, especially if this is something that is mentioned sporadically by a single witness. I don't know whether my arguments are right or not but I'm just simply stating our views on this particular matter. And not only did we view it like that, but this is also the way we explained it to our client. So the first point of departure was it's not in the indictment, I do not consider myself to be charged. Then witnesses came who spoke in the court-room, and then we heard the Prosecutor say that testimony by -- or witness statements were provided in time, you could have prepared, we wrote down to which counts of the indictment that referred to so you did not really discharge your duties properly, and you did not pay attention to that. Therefore, that is your failure. It's perhaps a strategy by the Prosecution which brings the Defence into a very difficult position. The Prosecutor stated that the witness statements were provided in time. We were not given a witness statement. We were given thousands of witness statements which, from the very outset, 80 per cent of which they did not plan to bring to trial. We were faced with tonnes of paper, and perhaps amongst those piles of paper there was a witness statement that was planned to be used in the trial. So first of all, when it is says [as interpreted] that the information was received through witness statements, I don't believe that that kind of warning or information was provided to us in the proper way, because we were constantly buried under new witness statements. This went on practically until yesterday. The Prosecution knows that the Defence is in a weaker position. There is only two of us and papers kept arriving and we had to sort through all of them. However, for example, we were provided with a witness statement who then becomes perhaps a key witness, turned into key witness from an anonymous witness, and then it is stated that each count is covered by particular witness statements. Witnesses here testify about everything, however. They refer to each count in the indictment. So I am not in a position to accept an argument that something has been clarified when, for Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. example, such and such a witness comes and that they will testify to all counts of the indictment, or perhaps to 100 per cent of the indictment, and then we have this witness come to the court-room, we listen to them and they say, one day, I don't know whether this was in the fall or in the spring, somebody beat me up, I don't know whether that was here or there, I don't remember who that was with, I don't know any more whether Martinovic was there or not, perhaps he was there, I heard -- well, as far as I'm concerned, I don't consider that that witness is charging me of anything. I cannot focus. On the other hand, I have a very complex indictment, a very complex indictment, containing hundreds of incidents. Well, not hundreds of incidents but a large number of incidents. It's a cumulative indictment with alternative charging. For one act of commission, there are five different qualifications. How -- well, I, not I but the Defence has to be focused. With killing, you have wooden rifles, you have this, you have that, how can I think then that I am charged by a witness who, for example, states that he was -- that some professor was beaten, somebody says, well, I don't know if that's that professor. I don't have the right information. So I'm claiming three things: It was not in the indictment; I was not informed in a timely manner that that's what I would be charged with; and then even when a witness is brought here I'm not given elements in order to put up a defence. I don't know the place. I don't know the event. I can find nothing out from that witness in order to organise an investigation. He doesn't tell me who he was with so I can look for those witnesses. Were you there on that day? It's not there. So -- and in particular, what is a problem in all of that, it's just a small indication, it's a small line, there is -- it's one or 200 metres long, then there is another unit farther along, and then there is a third unit, and witnesses are coming every day and they don't remember whether it's this unit or that unit. But anyway, I don't want to tire you any further. I believe that we were not informed in the manner that was proper. I believe that it is not all right that I must consider witness statement to be an indictment, and it's not all right for me to have to investigate what I'm charged with up until the last day, which witness is charging me with what? And these are the reasons why, in all of these counts we believe that we were not charged. We could not have put up a defence because we did not have the relevant elements. I still have a few things to cover briefly. Paragraph 143, order to transfer -- transform a private facility to the Vinko Skrobo command post. This is just one document out of a hundred that were seen here. The witness said one day I was repairing something, I was cleaning and repairing a damaged building. I don't know if we are talking about unlawful labour. Suddenly we find out that after this witness, this building will just happen to have two command offices there. I find out that I have finished indictment, and then in the judgement, I read that Martinovic ordered that private facilities or buildings be turned into military facilities, and we didn't feel that we were charged in the way that it was presented there. Paragraph 184, three incidents of mistreatment of prisoners. I also consider that I was not charged for this. Why? This is a typical example when we cannot really put up a defence. We don't know when, we don't know how, we don't know where, we don't know who, we don't have the basic information. Why wasn't this in the indictment? Well, nobody can specify that properly. This is really -- it's not possible to write an indictment around this. Was the Prosecution -- were the Prosecution in a position to do that, and this is clear to any reasonable man, they would have done that, but how could they have written it when they don't have the required elements that we seek? We don't know what we are accused of. And then we have some kind of testimony here, and then ultimately it turns out that we are charged for something like that. This is absolutely unacceptable to me, all of these things. I just felt that I was not charged for that. Paragraph 417, unlawful transfer. We have the situation that I mentioned. This is an event from the 29th of September, 1993. I don't feel accused or charged with that event, but there is one witness who came. He will tell us that he was expelled and transferred across the lines. And then I have a charge for this. The Prosecutor said 600 people were expelled across that line. Where are the witnesses? There was just one witness. Where are these 600 people? For some counts, ten people were brought. It's clear to everyone that 80 per cent of witnesses who appeared here were quite irrelevant. They don't appear anywhere in the judgement. Anyway, what kind of a charge is this? 600 people were allegedly expelled by Martinovic and then he's to be sentenced on the basis of one witness who provided the wrong testimony. Where did he make a mistake? He made a mistake just like anybody else could make a mistake. He was in a different place. He was not in the area of his unit. The witness made a mistake and the Trial Chamber made a mistake. Why did the Trial Chamber make a mistake? The witness said I was, we were expelled to a different or transferred to a different part of town near the pulmonary hospital. Let's remember that hospital. Martinovic held the line near the health centre. The facility was called the health centre. These are two different facilities, and they were in the areas of responsibility of two different units. So the witness said, I was transferred to the pulmonary hospital. I think, great, that is the Benko Penavic unit. What do we care? However, the Trial Chamber mixed up the terms, the pulmonary hospital and the medical centre, and they drew their conclusion based on that. According to the Trial Chamber, according to the place where they were displaced, we conclude that this happened in Martinovic's area of responsibility. This is a typical mistake and this is how we were charged for the expulsion of 600 people. Paragraphs 431, 4 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the number of the two other paragraphs.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are counts about the plunder of Martinovic's soldiers and here is the proof. Systematic plunder, there were three witnesses. On this count, there was some Witness F, who also testified about a hundred different counts, wooden rifles, unlawful labour, practically everything in the indictment, and he also in a couple of sentences he mentioned something about the -- actually, he focused on the wooden rifles but in a couple of sentences he also talked about a little bit of looting, plunder, and then this will appear in the judgement. Let's see how this actually happened. Let's just find this particular point. Yes. This witness who according to his statement holds Martinovic responsible for plunder. He says, well, I was with some soldiers, we were in some place, I don't know which place, I don't know the town, and so on and so forth. And the Prosecutor asked him, did you see Martinovic there? I did not. Were these units -- soldiers from his unit? Yes, I think there were. Did he know about this? He said, well, I really couldn't be sure. Well, of course he couldn't be sure. Nobody could be sure. For example, such testimony we had. There was another witness, Witness OO. Witness OO: I don't know any specific information. There was plunder somewhere. The soldiers were somewhere but it wasn't checked, where, when, how, what? And then of course there were other mistakes which are evident right away. Witness F stated, I claim that soldiers from Martinovic's unit took me for plunder and I went to plunder with them. Do you know the name of the soldier who took you? Answer: Yes. That is a soldier named Zubac. I know him personally. Do you know where you were? I do know. Show it on the map. He showed it on the map. It's an area called Aleksica Kuca. And now let's take out the list of soldiers of Martinovic's unit. There is no Zubac, there is no Zubac. There is a cook called Zradka Zubac [phoen] but he probably didn't mean her. But in the area of Aleksica Kuca which he indicated as the place where he went looting, which was under the responsibility of Benko Penavic unit, there was a soldier called Mario Zubac there and he probably meant him. And we did ask him during the hearing, are you thinking of Mario Zubac? He said, I don't know but he was Zubac. However, Martinovic was convicted of that, that in Aleksica Kuca, his soldier Zubac, a soldier he did not have, ordered plunder. These are all these paragraphs where I believe that the indictment is imprecise and indistinct, and I just simply feel that we are not charged in the proper way. Even a layman could clearly come to this conclusion. I'm not sure about the standards which we could apply here. This is talking about these groups. How much time do I have left? Very well, I still have five minutes. In relation to other questions, there was a question here, let us explain, what did we mean when we said that cumulative charging requires the proof of intent. And perhaps we were unclear there. From the very beginning, we were opposed to cumulative and alternative charging. We know what the practice is and that this is accepted but we had to express our position on this. I do not want to elaborate too much on this, but let us just take the example of killing, convicted of -- or charged with killing under 13 and 14 counts in the indictment and the other count was wilful killing. The elements of this criminal act are the same. We have one killing, this is my thinking, and we are prosecuting a person for two. And how do we believe that this can be resolved when one single act implies the commission of several crimes? We believe that the aggravated crime can be prosecuted in that case. If in this specific situation the Trial Chamber believed that there were conditions in order to convict under Article 5 and Article 2, we believe that it can convict only for the graver crime and that the lesser crime is subsumed in the graver, more serious crime, and we believe that this is very important. This is also important when we are talking about the international nature of the conflict. We will see whether it was proved the intent of participating in an international conflict was proved. If this intent was not proved, please let's not then take the cumulative approach, simply when this approach is taken, it should not be taken if a more serious criminal act can include a lesser criminal act. Why do we insist on this cumulative aspect of charging? When we are talking about expulsions and persecution, we have so many similar acts here and we just don't know how to go about it. It's not so complicated regarding the legal qualifications but we have cumulative witnesses here. We have Witness WW whom we considered as irrelevant. He piled up in his statement so many things we didn't even know we were charged for. He piled up a hundred of different acts, the commission of expulsion and I don't know what else. We believe that cumulative charging leads to making one actual event and one witness to a particular type of indictment and then a kind of judgement or conviction that we simply cannot understand where Martinovic would be charged for two murders when actually only just one occurred. Let me just see what else there is of these questions. There was one question where the Trial Chamber -- well, perhaps I could just say something that I feel important -- that is important about alternative charging. Why are we opposed to the alternative charging? These are also in reference to items 13 and 14. The Prosecution charges in the alternative killing, Count 13, or alternatively Count 16, cruel treatment, and Count 17, the infliction of grave suffering. The indictment begins, we -- different arguments are brought out and then the Trial Chamber says in the course of the proceedings, evidence is brought and then at the end of the proceedings, there is alternative charging and that will stay. Why do we think now about this alternative charging? We believe, and we are requesting and we would like to see -- we would like to defend our position. If the Prosecution left alternative charging until the end of the proceedings, I believe that the Prosecutor is still in doubt about exactly which criminal acts the accused committed. We believe that in that case the Trial Chamber cannot try the accused for the graver crimes. It has to go in favour of the accused and try him for the lesser charges. There has to be a legal standard. When the Prosecution is proceeding with some kind of open doubt, then the Trial Chamber has to try for the lesser crime. That is our position regarding alternative charging. If I have no more time left, I am finished. I have stated all the most important things that I wish to say, and I thank you very much for your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Par. [B/C/S on channel 4].

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the translation from B/C/S into English comes on channel 4. It appears that the English without translation comes on channel 1. I don't know if that will assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, I was saying we can now move on to the response of the Prosecution. Prosecution will have half an hour this evening to start the response, and then the response will continue tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, I will be responding to two of the grounds of appeal that were argued this morning. I hope that I will finish my response to the first one, which is international armed conflict, before we retire today and then, if necessary, address the issue of Nenad Harmandzic, the murder, tomorrow morning, and then my colleagues will address the other issues that remain. With respect to the ground of appeal relating to the international Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. armed conflict, I will address one issue that was raised by the Appellant, and that's the factual claim in their brief that Mr. Martinovic did not have any knowledge, awareness or intention required by this Tribunal's law to be found guilty of Article 2 crimes. I would raise one -- well, two preliminary questions. The first one is the issue of the ground of appeal which in my submission appeared to be a factual one, not a legal one, and that the issue raised now is as a result of the intervening decision in the Appeals Chamber in the Kordic and Cerkez case, and therefore I will at the end of my submissions on this issue indicate that the parties, in particular the Prosecution request this now, that the parties be permitted to brief this issue. It was not in the brief of the Appellant, it was not in the Prosecution's response brief. It wasn't an issue until the Kordic Appeals Chamber decision in December of 2004. I will, in any event, address the issues in summary form at this time to give you the Prosecution's position, but if I may say so, it will be in summary form as this matter hasn't been briefed fully. The preliminary legal question is, simply put, whether or not there is a requirement for a contextual element of international armed conflict for there to be a mens rea component of awareness. That preliminary legal question is, according to the Appellant, answered in paragraph 311 of the Kordic Appeals Chamber judgement. If I could just, as background, indicate that the Kordic Appeals Chamber judgement was based on submissions that were on the principle of nullum crimen sine lege, and the decision was based on the principle of nullum crimen sine lege. In that case, there was no argument on the mental element necessary for international armed conflict. It wasn't briefed. In fact, in the submissions by counsel for Mr. Kordic, on May the 17th, 2004, at page 319 of the hearing, the argument put forward by the Appellant on nullum crimen sine lege was that the offence under Article 2 could only fall within the jurisdiction of the Tribunal if the offence was recognised as a form of liability under customary international law as it existed at the time the offence was committed. The Appellant did not argue that there is a mental element requirement for international armed conflict. The decision in Kordic, if accepted to stand for the proposition put forward by my friend, essentially in the Prosecution's submission, overrules previous judgements of this Appeals Chamber. The Tadic Appeals Chamber essentially and implicitly, though not addressing the issue directly, established the liability of Mr. Tadic on an objective standard. In the Celebici Appeals Chamber decision, the Celebici Appeals Chamber determined that international armed conflict was established objectively and then determined that the regime of the Geneva Conventions found under Article 2 applied and convicted the Appellants in that case as in Tadic under Article 2 with no finding of a factual awareness of the circumstances related to armed conflict. As well, it's interesting to note that in the Kordic and Cerkez Appeals Chamber, if you accept the Appellant's submission that this created an awareness element, in paragraph 311, Mr. Cerkez was convicted under Count 30 for Article 2 charges of the Statute, and he was convicted for crimes committed in the municipality of Vitez, in the town of Vitez, in relation to the detention crimes in Vitez for which he was the commander. As far as I could see, there was no findings by the Appeals Chamber that Mr. Cerkez had knowledge of the factual circumstances surrounding the nature of the conflict in terms of an international armed conflict. At least in my review of the judgement I could not find anything that would support the conclusion that the previous findings in paragraph 311 required that factual finding, and that the Chamber then found those factual findings to support the conviction which was upheld on appeal. Second, paragraph 311 in the determination of the -- what I submit is an actual mens rea element was decided in the context of the principle of nullum crimen sine lege. And it's the Prosecution's submission that this is not a requirement of nullum crimen and that nullum crimen sine lege encompasses essentially two components. First, the prohibition against ex post facto laws, and secondly, the foreseeability and accessibility of the law by the accused. What's interesting is that the foreseeability and accessibility requirement is an objective one. It's whether or not a person could have known that the conduct was criminal and that the essence of the offence, the very essence of the offence could have been foreseen. If nullum crimen is satisfied by an objective element, I fail to see, in my respectful submission, how nullum crimen would require a subjective element going to the mens rea. The nullum crimen requirement is that an accused must have reasonably known at the time that that conduct is considered criminalised, not that the mens rea components have been established and that at the time he's committing the offence he must have a certain awareness which the Prosecution must prove for a conviction. Lastly I would note on this issue that even if Kordic was to stand for the proposition that it overturned the implicit findings in both Celebici and Tadic, without reasons and without referring to those decisions, there is, with respect, at least I'm unaware of any support for the proposition, that a perpetrator to be held liable is required to know the -- as a context element, the character of the armed conflict. Even looking to the ICC Statute, Article 8, Article 8 of the ICC Statute specifically states in the introduction to the elements that: "There is no requirement for awareness by the perpetrator of the facts that established the character of the conflict as international or non-international. Commentators on the elements of the ICC Statute have indicated that requiring a perpetrator to know that the character of a certain conflict and requiring the Prosecutor to prove such knowledge would have been too high a threshold not required by existing law." That's the book by Mr. Lee, Roy Lee, The International Criminal Court, Element of Crimes and Rules of Procedure. Another commentator, Mr. Knut Dormann, in his book Elements of War Crimes under the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court writes that: "The requirement that perpetrator be aware of the international character of an armed conflict was rejected by almost all delegations." If leave is granted to brief this issue, the Prosecution will put these matters and this literature and the supporting material before the Court. If leave is not granted to brief this issue, further in written terms, the Prosecution still relies on its -- all its submissions it makes today. Third, the third point is that the Trial Chamber concluded that there was no requirement of a mens rea component in relation to the international nature of the armed conflict. In fact, as I'm sure you're aware, in the Rule 98 bis decision it was raised by the Appellant at the Rule 98 bis stage that there was no evidence to demonstrate that the Appellant had an awareness or knowledge or intention in relation to the international armed conflict. And in that decision, on motion for acquittal of February 28th, 2002, the Trial Chamber said that it was not required. And that was the Prosecution's position throughout the case. So the characterisation that I may have interpreted from my friend that the Prosecution's position in not presenting any evidence of Mr. Martinovic's knowledge of the character of the armed conflict somehow reflected that there was no evidence is, quite frankly, not the issue. This Appeals Chamber in Blaskic has held that when there is an error of law the Chamber itself becomes the trier of fact. Now though the Court has cautioned against that obviously it has held in Blaskic that it would look at all the evidence at a -- on a reasonable doubt standard. If Kordic does stand for the proposition, which of course we submit it shouldn't be interpreted that way, that there is now in the jurisprudence a mens rea component, and that the Trial Chamber was in error, it then falls upon this Chamber to determine whether on the evidence before the Trial Chamber, there was sufficient facts to uphold the convictions under Article 2. And in that regard, I will refer you now to the evidence that was before the Trial Chamber and some of those findings in support of the conclusion that they were -- both Appellants, that is -- were aware of the factual circumstances of the international character of the armed conflict. Of course, I'm sure Your Honours appreciate that that's only if this Court finds that Kordic stands for the proposition that it's a requirement. I will now make submissions in relation to both Appellants, and I just wanted to let my learned colleagues for Mr. Naletilic know as I indicated earlier, that as the Defence for Mr. Martinovic raised this issue and as the issue affects both of them, I've attempted to indicate that I would refer to the facts at the hearing, and I have no objection if the Court so leaves and if the Appellant so requires that they be given the opportunity, that is counsel for Mr. Naletilic as well, to respond shortly to the facts I will put forward, only as a matter of fairness since they haven't addressed this issue because I'm raising it now in relation to the Martinovic appeal. Let me give you some of the background, some of the context elements. The Court found at paragraphs 192 and 193, referring to 36 exhibits and 12 witnesses, the presence and direct intervention of the Croatian army, that's the term HV, in Bosnia-Herzegovina and in particularly in the area of Mostar in 1993. The Trial Chamber at paragraph 193 said that the HV troops took part in the crimes committed against the Muslims, including in Mostar. There are 14 different witnesses who testified that a Croatian army Brigade known as the Tigers was in the Mostar region, including at the Heliodrom detention centre. A number of witnesses testified that an HV Brigade known as the Thunders were also in Herzegovina and in the Mostar region. The Trial Chamber at paragraph 193 noted that several witnesses testified that these HV units were actually stationed at the Heliodrom detention centre during the relevant time periods in the indictment. And I note the previous finding that some of the same victims who were taken out by the Convicts' Battalion, including Mr. Martinovic's Brigade, were also signed out at other times by the Croatian army units from the Heliodrom. I ask you to recall that both Mr. Naletilic and Mr. Martinovic themselves personally went to the Heliodrom on numerous occasions and were identified by witnesses being present there. This is in paragraphs 432 to 436 of the trial judgement. It's submitted that it's not logical that the detainees at the Heliodrom would know of the fact that HV units and that those HV units are stationed at the Heliodrom and are operating in Mostar but the influential head of the Convicts' Battalion and his subcommander in the Mostar region would be ignorant of this fact. Let me take you through the judgement for a few moments, recognising the time that I have. If I can ask you to turn to page 193, or I'll simply cite to the evidence and the findings, if you wish. Paragraph 193 in the second sentence of the judgement found at page 65 says the -- talking about the HV troops, says those HV soldiers belong to different units and were based in different locations and at times took part in the crimes committed against the Muslim population. If you turn to footnote 533, which is at least in my judgement on the next page, it says Witness AE testified that early on the 9th of May 1993, Muslim civilians were arrested by soldiers wearing both HV and HVO uniforms and insignias. A former member of the Convicts' Battalion, witness Falk Simang, testified that HV soldiers took part to the evictions of Muslims in Mostar together with the HVO. That's on the 9th. You'll see in paragraph 534, sorry, footnote 534, the Court also notes halfway through that footnote an exhibit, PP373, according to which the HV participated in the conflict in Mostar on May the 9th, 1993, and lists the exhibits in support of that finding. Now, if I can ask you to turn to the Court's finding related to the attack on May 9th, the one they've just referred to, if I can ask you to turn to paragraph 145 of the judgement. Paragraph 145 talks about two witnesses who were members of the Convicts' Battalion, and the operation in Mostar on the 9th of May. The last sentence reads: "According to witness Ralf Mrachacz, Mladen Naletilic had command authority over the KB during all operations in Mostar." Now, if I can take you to footnote -- the footnote 427, at the very, very end, the last sentence: "The Trial Chamber finds that the testimonies of witnesses Falk Simang and Ralf Mrachacz reliable and credible." Now, let's look at footnote 428 in relation to the testimony of these two witnesses who have been found reliable and credible. Witness Falk Simang also testified about a second operation in Mostar. He states that Mladen Naletilic assigned him to a group of BH Croats with whom he marched into Mostar to cleanse one side of the city. He further testified that: "All units who were under General Tuta's order plus from the HV took part in the operation and that the Supreme Commander for us was General Tuta." The Court has found in my respectful submission that not only were there troops in Mostar, not only were they Croatian troops stationed at the Heliodrom which in the Prosecution submissions one could draw an inference of knowledge but the Court actually found that they were operating in conjunction with the Convicts' Battalion and in one operation under Tuta, General Tuta's command. There were other relevant findings, and I won't take you through the judgement to them; I'll just note them. At paragraph 199 of the Trial Chamber judgement, footnote 548, the witness Mrachacz confirmed that most of the Convicts' Battalion equipment was coming from Croatia. Now, I'll ask you to recall that Mrachacz was a mercenary who was a member of the Convicts' Battalion. He didn't speak the language particularly well, and he was in knowledge accepted by the Trial Chamber as credible, that he knew that the equipment was coming from Croatia and it would be somewhat incredible that a soldier of the Convicts' Battalion would know about it but the commander of the Convicts' Battalion and his subcommander would have no idea. In footnote 553, again referring to Mrachacz's testimony, Mrachacz testified that as a member of the Convicts' Battalion he was paid in Croatian money that was brought from Croatia by Naletilic. Exhibit P327, (redacted), it states that Naletilic asked Boban and Tudjman for permission to create his own anti-terrorist unit. And lastly, the Prosecution in its closing brief referred to Exhibit P558, which was a handwritten letter apparently from Naletilic to the Croatian Minister of Defence, Gojko Susak, requesting that certain soldiers be permitted to join him in action. It's respectfully submitted that the only reasonable conclusion on not only the evidence but the facts as found would be that if you determine it that it's a requirement, the evidence is conclusive that Mr. Naletilic had the awareness of factual circumstances, and I note that the Kordic Appeals Chamber judgement doesn't indicate what is meant by factual circumstances, whether it's the factual circumstances or just some factual circumstances. It uses as an example the involvement of troops from another country. As you're aware, international armed conflict can be determined on two bases, both the involvement of troops but also overall control, and in this case, there is sufficient evidence to show on both aspects that Mr. Naletilic was involved -- I'm sorry, was aware. If I could in the last five minutes try and finish in relation to the facts against Mr. Martinovic. Once again, I'm sorry it appears the court reporter wasn't getting my submissions. I'm sorry, it was in B/C/S, which probably isn't me as my language skills aren't that good. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: Is that okay now?

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As I said, I'd ask that you please take into consideration all my previous submissions and the previous findings that I've already referred to. I will now only address specifically additional ones in relation to Mr. Martinovic. Start by recalling a finding of the Trial Chamber at paragraph 195, and at paragraph 195 the Trial Chamber found that the Republic of Croatia in fact organised the sending of the vast majority of the HV troops in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Now you may recall that Witness Simang, Witness Knudsen and Witness QQ were all sent from Croatia and they all ended up in the Convicts' Battalion, and two of them ended up in Mr. Martinovic's battalion. Witness Knudsen testified, at transcript pages 5591 to 5599, that he was in Zagreb with Witness Q and that they were approached about going to Bosnia. They had been previously been involved in conflict including in Bosnia. They were told to see a gentleman by the name of Branko Barbic who they contacted. Mr. Barbic is a military attache for the Parliament of Croatia. They went and saw Mr. Barbic and they met him at the Croatian parliament. Witness Allan Knudsen indicated that he took them into his office at the Croatian parliament and upon deciding to send them to Mostar, he gave them a letter and that letter was that all units in Croatia and Bosnia were to help them to get to Mostar where they were to join the HVO. In fact, Mr. Knudsen testified that the HV army in Croatia provided accommodation and transportation to get them there. Upon their arrival in Mostar, which is in the beginning of September, Mr. Knudsen produced the signed document from Branko Barbic from the Parliament of Croatia to Vinko Martinovic, and as Witness QQ testified, he wasn't sure that Mr. Martinovic wanted to accept them at first but on the basis of the document that he was given, he accepted them. In fact, as a result they were assigned an apartment in Mostar. Mr. Knudsen also testifies that in mid-September he was injured and went back to Denmark. After his recovery he returned in October, returned to the Croatian parliament, met with Mr. Barbic, received a letter from him which allowed him to return and returned to Mr. Martinovic's brigade. The second time he went back he kept the letter, and that letter is Exhibit 658. And the letter from Mr. Barbic is addressed to both the Croatian army and the Bosnian Croat army, and it states that Mr. Knudsen is to be sent to one of "our" units in Mostar. It's submitted it's obvious that Mr. Martinovic, in light of the contextual evidence I've referred to and the involvement of the HV in Mostar, their operations on the 9th, their fact that they are at the Heliodrom or Mr. Martinovic sends his troops -- soldiers to collect prisoners and the fact that he's there himself on occasion is overwhelming evidence that he was aware of the troops in Mostar and their involvement in the Bosnian Croat war. As you know, the Court concluded that Mr. Martinovic was involved in the action on May the 9th and was carrying out evictions. The HV units in combat in Mostar in May and there were HV soldiers involved in the evictions. The Court doesn't find to those evictions are the same ones that Mr. Martinovic was involved in, to be fair, but just the evictions in May. I also note that in relation to the HV units stationed at the Heliodrom, the Heliodrom logbook, Exhibit P601.1, has an entry for the 17th of September 1993. That's the day when detainees were removed for the purposes of forced labour. The Court found that was the date of the wooden rifle incident. In the logbook there is an entry where detainees were taken by the Vinko Skrobo Brigade, which is Mr. Martinovic's brigade, and the next entry below has an entry that the HV Brigade, the Tigers, are signing out detainees for forced labour on the same day. Clearly indicates that they are involved at the same time, at the same place. Witness OO testified at transcript page 5939 that while he was engaged in forced labour at Santiceva Street, which is the street that's not in Mr. Martinovic's zone of responsibility but in the next one, that there were HV units stationed at that area of responsibility. If there are HV units stationed at the area of responsibility close to Mr. Martinovic's in a military operation, I'd submit that it's inconceivable that he wouldn't know who the troops were that were beside him. Mr. Knudsen also testified that he saw HV Croatian army vehicles in front of the headquarters of Vinko Martinovic. That's at paragraph T5662. And also Mrachacz testimony I mentioned earlier is applicable, which is that the Convicts' Battalion equipment supplies and salary came from Croatia, and the Convicts' Battalion included Mr. Martinovic. So on the basis of that evidence, it's submitted that the only reasonable conclusion is that they both were aware of the factual circumstances. The Prosecution of course maintains its original position: (1), that it's not a requirement; and (2), that if the Court in Kordic held it is a requirement, that based on the Aleksovski Appeals Chamber decision, which indicated where a decision is made per incuriam, that it is open to this court to reconsider it on the basis that there are cogent reasons. In my respectful submission, if the Kordic Appeals Chamber judgement is interpreted as my friends have interpreted it, as there are no reasons given for the creation of a mens rea element, as the case implicitly overturns the findings in Tadic and Celebici, as there were no submissions on this issue by the parties, I would respectfully submit that the parties in this case be permitted to brief this issue as it was raised for the first time during oral submissions. Thank you for your patience. I see I'm just a little bit over. That ends the submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Farrell. I have found there was something to redact. A document was mentioned that was under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. FARRELL
utterances.text: Thank you. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE POCAR
utterances.text: We will take care of that. This will conclude the hearing for today. We will now adjourn and continue tomorrow morning at 9.00 with the continued response by the Prosecution. They will be followed by the reply by Martinovic. And then we will continue according to the Scheduling Order of 16 of September 2005. The hearing stands adjourned.
